IN obedience to an order of the Grand Lodge of this· State, pas~cd
May 14th, A. L. 5858, the third volume of its proceedings, embracing
the transactions of the years 5857 and 5858, is now bound in a manner uniform with the preceding ones, and presented for the use 1Jf the
Lodges and brethren. A new and copious index has been prepared ;
and as no labor ha~ been spared, either in the original preparation of
the matter for and its progress through tlie press, or in the superintendence of its present arrangement, it is hoped that it may meet the
approbation of the Craft, and be deemed worthy the high position
which the Grand Lodge of California now occupies among the similar
bodies of the world.
If this method of perpetuat.ilig our records be continued, it is
scarcely possible that the history Gf Masonry in this State can become
obliterated or obscure. Jlew, if aay, of the Grand Lodges now e:r.isting, can present such a series of p11blications : and the undersigned
feels a double pleasure in having originated the present system for preserving the annals of Masonry here, and in having thus far been so
well supported by the Grand J.oodge in carrying it into effect.

ALEX. G. ABELL,
Grand Sem-etary.

Our acknowledgments are first due to our Supreme Grand Master for his protection during the past year, and for the many evidences which he has afforded us
of his superintending care. In the oblations which we have offered for bis acceptance, we have pledged ourselves to the promotion of thl\t peace und harmony which

we have besought him should pervade our councils; and let us not forget that he
will hold us iwcounta.ble for any act of ours which may be calculated to mar their
eftlcacy, and to introduce confusion and misrule. Let the general tenor of
our deportment be conducive to the legitimate purposes of our assemblage,
t o the eradication o~ evil, and to the attainment of good; and in their accomplishment let us see that our councils be chracterised by that prudent and deliberative action which seldom fails to result from an enlightened andjust course of
policy ; and above all, that they bear the impress of the ennobling virtues of forhearance and self-sacrifice, wherever they may be needed to promote peace and
harmony and secure the greatest amouut of good to the greatest number. Let us
bear these things in mind, my brethren,-tbat Masonry inculcates forbearance,
an<l rejoices in the doctrine of an expansirn charity; and let the line of our conduct
lie in accordance with these suggestions.
Another year has passed away. It has passed as the wind passeth, and like the
wind when the wings of the tempest have been spread and its power invoked, it
has left traces of its violence , while sweeping away the pestilential vapors that
hovered OYer it.s pathway. Would that itseYils bad all passed along with it, and
that thl.l good alone remained. Then might we not be called upon to deplore the
one, while coutemplating the other, as seen through the medium of past events,
aml the impress of their tracings upon . the lineaments of the developing future.
Another year has passed away. The sound of its whirl of stirring incident~
has tlied in lingering echoes beneath the mausoleum of ages. But its history baB
been written. 'fhe record of its changeless events bas been laid up in the world's
archives, to he brought forth when tbe day of retribution shall come- when tlie
myriad~ who have trodden the earth .shall be aroused from their deep slumbers when the juRt and the unjust, the oppret;Sed 11nd the oppressor, the murderer and
his victim, shllll stand face to face before a tribunal where iajusticc will find no
a!hocate ; where the yoke of the oppressor will lie broken beucath the feet of th~
oppre8sed ; where the baud of tho assnssin will be pRlsied and powerless forever ;
u.ntl there will be no leRgue of iniquity to shield the confederates of crime. With
the yt>ar that has passed, have gone 11lso t he loved and the lost ofour own number.
'f hcy have been but few, but many have lu.mented their fate. Who is there among

there that ever knew, and did not love him ? Others too, whose 1mmes 11re written upon the tablets of our hearts, have trodden the rnlley of the shadow of death
~ince last we met. While on the one band the sih-er cord was gently loosed by
t.he hlight of disease, and the pitcher noii;elessly broken at the fount11in, on the

of violence, 11nd the wheel was broken at the cist.ern ere the half of its evolution~
hud been made. May they rest in peace ; for their winter of death has pass1:d away,
and we luwe au abiding hope that they have awakened to newueAA of life, in the
g-enial warmth of tb11t bright and happy spirit-land whither they bai•e b'Onl'.

As regards our own Lodges, their interference with one another's jurisdictional

I have had occasion to observe that our Grand Lodge has not always exercised
due discrimination in ordering Charters for new Lodges, and has sometimes granted them where it appears to me that it would have been better to have required
another year's probation. I should think it improper as well as impolitic, to
hurry a Lodge to maturity with the evidences before us of its probationary state
not having been such as to render advisable such a procedure. In this connection, I would remark in reference to Lodges under Dispensation, that I agree
with the Grand Lodge that they are but " temporary and inchoate bodies, and
not entitled to representation in the Grand Lodge, and those who work them do
not forfeit their membership thereby in any other Lodge, while it so continues";
but I do not believe in the propriety or correctness of the principle of 11U&peruli11g
their membership in the chartered Lodges of which they may be members, because they have voluntnrily assumed responsibilities elsewhere. I think
it an injudicious interference with the lawfully incurred responsibility of the individual, as well as with the local regulations of his Lodge. I would rather let him
enjoy his privileges and pay his dues, and if he sees proper to contribute of his
means to the support of a rtew Lodge in addition thereto, let him do so-it is his
own affair and should, I think, be left to his own will. It seems to me that
where we can do so with propriety, we should encourage voluntary contributions
to the treeauries of our Lodges, which are drawn upon so freely for charitable
purposes, rather than to pursue n. course which would have a tendency to leSBen
~hem.

The Grand Secretary presented his Annual Report, as follows : To the M:. W: . Grand Lodge qf California: The undersigned again presents the Annual Report required by the Constitution
from the Grand Secretary.
Immediately after the close of the last Communication, he officially informed
Bros. L. J. Cz.lPK.lY, JESSJ: MORRILL, and A. Hu.a, of the action of the Grand
Lodge by which they were severally restored to the rights and privileges of Masonry; and, in accordance with the instructions given, addressed a letter to the
Grand Lodge of Germany, in 1eply to the communication thence received the pre·
ceding year. Both papers are herewith submitted. Letters were also transmitted
to the former Master of Parific Lodge, at Valparaiso, Chile, and to tlit Grand
Lodge of Massachusetts, enclosing the resolutions adopted at the last session in re·
lation to that Lodge, formerly under this jurisdiction; an•l the order of the Grand
Lodge, directing the return of fift,v·six dollars to foe Grand Lodge of New Jeraey,
has been complied with, as will be seen by the acknowledgemeut of ita receipt
contained in a letter from Past Grand Master Edward Stewart, herewith presented.
In compliance with the resolution passed last year, parchment has been procured
from New York, and one hundred blank Charters have been prepared, which are
no"w offered for inspection. The various Grand Secretaries in the United States
have again been requested to furnish us with the back publications of their tran11actions, and a considerable number have been received in addition to tho1e reported
at the last Communication,, which have been bound 11.nd placed in the library. A
.:omplete edition of the "~1asonic Review," by Bro. C. Moore, of Cincinnati, com·
prising fifteen \'Olumes, has also been received.
Fifteen hundred copies of the proceedings at your last meeting were pFinted and
distributed as usual, with the exception of five hundred reserved for binding, and
those required for use at your present session; and the undersigned having on hi1
own account completed the republication of the transactions of this Grand Lodge
from its organization to and including the year 1854, again urges upon your attention the propriety and utility of having those of 1855 and 18:16, now on hand,
bound in a similar manner, and sold to the Lodges and Masons in the State at such
price as shall cover the cost of their printing and binding. There are now on hand
five hundred or more copies of each of those two years, which together would make
n volume of some four hundred and fifty pages, equaling in size that already published;
and as all the Lodges can now be supplied with the complete proceedings to 1854,
it is recommended, not only that those of 1855 and 1860 be thus prepared, but
that hereafter a similar number of copies be laid aside each year to be bound a1
often as a volume of suitable size shall have been completed. Not only can the existing Lodges then be furnished with a complete history of the Masonic transactions of this State, but each new Lodge hereafter created, r.11n at once be provided
with them all, at a price which shall remunerate the Grand Lodge for the di1burat·
ment necessary to accomplish this useful project.

The Grand Secretary further presented the following communication
from the Masonic Board of Relief of the city of San lfrancisco : - ·
1b the M.-. W.·. Grand Lodge of Oalifarnia: -

The Masonic Board of Relief of the city of San Francisco, believing that your
Most Worshipful Body will learn with pleasure of the success of its ministrations
in the cause of charity during the past year, have directed me to present to you
at this Communication, a brief statement of the causes which induced its establishment, of the plau of its organization, and of the results which have attended
its operations.
For some years past it has been notorious that the Lodges of this city were frequently imposed upon by successful applicants for charity to several of them in
succession, by those whom a proper opportunity for investigation would have exhibited as utterly unworthy to receive it ; and, that even in the cases of deserving
applicants, who were strangers, it was impossible that the Lodges, at a single
meeting, should be able sufficiently to understand them, to be enabled to discriminate wisely as to the amount and mode of the relief to be afforded. So evident
was this, that as early as the year 1854 an effort was made to institute au association of the Lodges here, similar to that now existing, but it failed to be carried
into effect, - not because the plan was disapproved, but because of a lack of energy and attention to conduct it to completion. In the following year it was
again proposed, and the result was a compact between five of the Lodges, with
an invitation to the others to become parties to it, should they feel so disposed.
This went iL1to operation from the first day of January, 1856, aml its principal
features, after a recitation of the causes which led to its formation, are that a
Board of Relief should be established, to be composed of' the Masters or presiding
officers of the Lodges assenting to it, to which all applications for assistance
from Masons, or the widows and children of Masons not belonging to any Lodge
in this city, shall be sent- that a fund for the relief of such applicants should be
provided by a tax upon the Lodges, parties to the compact, levied in the manner
hereinafter exhibited- that each member of the Board should report all cases requiring relief to that body at its regular weekly meetings, or to its chairman
during the recess - and that a report should he made to each of the assenting
LodgllB, twice in every year, detailing all the transactions of the Board during the
preceding six months.
The following was its second semi-annual Report, presented to the Lodges on
the thirty first day of December, 1857 ; and as lt gives a summary of the operations of the whole year preceding, it is exhibited as it was sent fo the constituent
bodies·:-

" REPORT OF THE MASONIC BOARD OF RELIE}' }'OR 1'HE YEAR ENDING THIRTY-FIRST
DECEMBER, 1856.
"1b the w: Master, Wardens and Brethren of
Lodge, No. " The Masonic Board of Relief of the city of San Francisco, in submitting this
its second semi-annual report to the several Lodges which have contributed to it~
establishment, take occasion at the close of the first year of its existence, to present, not only a summary of its proceedings during the past six months but a
full and detailed account of all its transactions during the entire year.
'
"As you have before been informed, the Masters respectively of California, Parfait~
Union, Occidental, Golden Gate, e.nd Mount Moriah Lodges, (these being the five which
first assented to the compact,) assembled on the thirty-first day of J annary 1856
and organized the Board by the election of Bro. ALEX. G. ABELJ. as Chairman'
Bro. A.G. RANDALL as Treasurer, and Bro. L. C. OWEN as Secretary, the othe;
two members being Bro. LEOPOLD LEVY and Bro. C. R. SAUNDERS. In accordance
with the second article of the compact, By-Laws were adopted for the government
of the Board, and for the regulation of the manner in which the charities confided
to its care should be administered ; the most material rules of which are that reg·
ular meetings shall be held once in each week- that relief shall be granted only
to regular and worthy Masons, their widows and children - that no sum greater
than fifty dollars shall be grantetl at one time, except in extreme cases and then
only by an unanimous vote - that the Treasurer shall give satisfactor7 bonds
for the faithful discharge of his trust, and shall make weekly reports o his receipts and disbursements - and that the Chairmim be empowered during the recess of the Boarcl to grant relief' in emergent cases to the extent of twenty dollars
reporting the c11se at the next meeting for approval.
'
"On the twenty-eighth day of February, Lebanon Lodge assented to the compact, and on the thirteenth day of the following month, Bro. JACOB MAYER appeared and signed it, thus making six of the city Lodges represented in the Board·
and we have now the additional pleasure of announcing that the only remaining
one, San Fmncisco, will become associated with us from the commencement of the
coming year- thus joining together the entire Brotherhood of the city, for the
accomplishment of the charitable purposes of our organization.
"The revenue of the Board, untler the terms of the compact, has been derived
as follows: " 1. From 11 general assessment of fifty cents for each member of every Lodge,
party to the compact.
"2. From u monthly asses1m1ent of ten cents for each member, ns before and
from a charge of' five dollars for each degree conferred.
'
"3. From such donations ns those charitably dispol!Ud, might from time to
time, present to the Board, to aid it in the performance of its duties ; and
"4. :From the power in cases of emergency, to levy un extra assessment on
the Lodges of twenty-five cents for each member.
" From thel!C sourc<Js the receipts during the ycnr just terminated, have been es

" Thns it will be seen that all the Lodges, parties to the compact, have paid

Thus it will be seen that five Lodges in the city of San Francisco have diE·
bursed in charity to sojourning brethren, their widows and orphans, within le!lll
than a year, the sum of $2484,50, besides the sums bestowed among the needy
and destitute of their own membership, these being expressly excluded from the
jurisdiction of the Board. The moneys thus additionally expended amount in
the aggregate to about $1500, making a total expenditure for benevolence of
nearly $4000 within the past twelve months.
Even this sum does not represent the whole amount which we should have been
compelled to disburse, had it not been for the charitable generosity of others ;
and we arc happy to have the opportunity thus to express the great obligations
we are under to the liberality of the Pacific llfail Steamship Company and the
California Steam Navigation Company. The first, through its agents in this cit.y,
Messrs. FORBES and BABCOCK, has always made generous deductions from their
usual charges, in the cases of pa~sengers sent home to the Atlantic States by this
Board; and the last, by its President, Bro. SAMCEL J. HENSLEY, has ever carried
free upon all their river steamers, those whom we were aiding to reach any part
of the interior.
The system has been found to work admirably. Time and opportunity is afforded by it to examine thoroughly the merits and requirements of each application ; and thus while imposition is prevented on the one hand, real need is certainly cared for on the other, and there is tolerable assurance that the funds
collected for charity are disbursed as wisely and judiciously as human fallibility
will permit.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
ALEX. G. ABELi,,

The Address of the Grand Master, like the papers of a. similar character which
emanated from bis predecessor, is an able and business-like production, detailing the prominent events which 'flave occurred during the vacation, and reviewing and commenting upon those matters about to be.brought to the attention of
the Grand Lodge. It will be recollected that we last year noticed a. vexed question, which for two or three years past bas occupied much of' the attention of
our brethren of Alabama,- the proposed partition, among the Lodges, of a fund
amounting to some $17,000, which had originally been intended for educational
purposes. This had finally been decided at the preceding Communication, and
11 division was ordered to be made ; but owing to some error in the proceedings,
the committee to whom the partition was entrusted were unable to proceed, and
the matter was a.gain in abeyance for another year. It would seem that the
Grand Master bad heretofore favored the project of distribution, but he now confe11ses ihat his views have undergone a. change in that respect, and that he believes, in the words of Grand Master CLOPTON, the year preceeding, that it would
be " almost tantamount to a waste of the funds." The Grand Lodge, however,
unfortunately as we think. entertained a different opinion, and the partition bas
been finally made ; thus dividing among more than two hundred Lodges a sum
which, had it been husbanded together, would have formed a splendid basis of a
fund for the endowment of some Masonic institution of charity or education.
Bro. Woon urges the necessity for a uniform system of work; nnd we remark
tbatat a later period a committee recommended the abolition of the present system of Grand Lecturers, and a return, as the lesser evil of the two, to the former
practice of exemplification at the Annual Communications. A considerable portion of the addreSA is devoted to a recommendation that steps be ta.ken for the
preparation of a wo;k upo~ the early history of Masonry i? that State, a._nd that
t!omething be done for the mcrease of the Grand Lodge Library. .The 1BSue of
seven Dispensations for new Lodges is recorded. He recommends the plan for
~ National.Confederation of Grnnd Lodges, and the Grand Lodge bas assented
by the adoption of the Articles prepared at Washington.

proportions. At our Communication in May, 1854, it was with all due solemnity

Lodges to see that their members exemplify the same iu their lives nnd conduct.''
Of what particular use this resolution, or others like it, can b.c'. we are unable to determine. Laws shou~d be laws, and not abstract opm1ons ; and it
seems worse than usele~ to lumber up the records with crude ideas, done into
wordy resolutions which bear no semblance of command, and which, if they
did, would be certain to be disobeyed. If we wish to prohibit a "retail traffic
in alcoholic liquors," or any unbending from " the stern morality of Masonrr.''
let us do so in terms, and provide a punishment for disobedience to the edict.
Or, better still, let us cease asserting, by resolution, an hundred things which
the moral law, the spirit and lessons of our Order, and the plainest common
sense hnd long since established. In brief. let ua not legiF!ate for Duncombe.

"We have yet to lenru that Masonry is especially a Christian institution, or that it is a
religious one at all; and while we doubt not lhat our own faith in 1he Divine authenticity
of the Holy Writings, both Old and New, is quite as implicit as lhat of our Christian
brother of lowa, we do not forget that there is a very large number of our brethren, os
~ood and worthy Masons as ourselves, who•e belief does not and r.annot extend so far.
The precepts of Masonry are moral, not religious, and a declaration of belief in God is
re';luired, not only for the reason given to the candidate upon his entry, but because there
is ~1ttle guarantee.t~at a m~n will obey the moral law, who does not give credence to the
ex1s.tence of a D1vme Arbiter of our future state of being. 'Masonry,' we are lold,

new test is not only an evident invasion of the primal law, but is n pafpable contradiction
of .the very history which we teach and P,rofess to believe. There is no law of Masonry
which should prevent the fraternity of Christian$, Jews and Mahometans; and that Brotherly Love, 'by which we are taught to regard the whole human species as one family,'
and .' whi~h conciliates true ~riendship among thosi; who might, (but for their Masonic
relat1onsh1p,) have ever remamed at a perpetual distance,' 1s the very foundation, life
and spirit of the institution.''
Bro. Sayre quotes the proceedings of Ohio in this respect at length, and then
thus exhibits the error of the proposition of that Grand Lodge by its own proceedings:"At the opening of the Communication of thP. Grand Lodge at which this report was
adopted, the Grand Master congratulated the brethren that 1\lasonry was spreading in
Turkey, and reviving in China. Now neither the Turks nor the Chinese believe in the
New 'testament. The Jews are everywhere admitted into our Lodges, but they do not
believe in the New Testament any more than the others. In fact, we are constantly
told that pure and unadulterated Masonry, or traces of it, may be found all over the
world- among the civilized and the savage - among those even who bave never heard
that lhere was such a thing as the Bible. Either lhese reports must be the merest fables,
or a belief in the authenticity of the Scriptures is not necessarv in the Mason. The
Jews, the followen of Confucius, and the Mahomedans, all reject either the New Testament, or the Old, or both, and yet we see no good reason why they should not be made
Masons. In fact, Blue Lodge Masonry has nothing whatever to do with the Bible. It is
not founded upon the Bible; for if it was, it would not be Masonr_y, but religion. Masonry' is merely a charitable institution. " # * * That some Masons may teach the
Divine authenticity of the Holy Scriptures is true, because some Masons are Christians;
but .Maa011ry does nothing. of t~e. sort., leavi.nir every ma.n to his ~wu opinions upon that
subject, as 11 does upon his polihcs, bis rehg1on, and his profe881on. Masonry ouly inquires if the candidate for mitiation possesses the proper physical qualities; if he be
free-born, of lawful age, under the tongue of good report, and properly vouched for :
then, if he believes in the existence of a God, he is a proper candidate for our sublime
mysteries.''

ARKANSAS.
The latest proceedings received from this Grand Lodge are those of its Annual Communication commenced at the City of Little Rock on the fifth day of
November, 1855- the M.·. W.·. NAT. G. SMITH, Grand Master, presiding, and tho
R.·. W.·. THos. D. MERRICK being (}rand Secretary.
The Grand Master notices the spread of Masonry among the tribes in the ad~oi~ing Indian terr.itory, an~ speaks highly of the advancement they have made
m its lessons and its practice. He states that he had revoked the suspension
inflicted 1Jy the Grand Lodge, at its last Communication, upon one of the subordinates which had refused to comply with an edict imposing a tax for the benefit of St. John's College, the Lodge having made due submission and paid up
the amount for which it was delinquent. Considerable space is given to the
subject of that Masonic institution of learning, and it would seem from the urgency of his appeal to the Fraternity in that State, as well as from the financial
reports in regard to the progress of collections on its account, that the project
has not advanced as happily as was desired. Yet it is still persisted in; and
though our brethren of Arkansas have not, like those of North Carolina last
year, built a college by resolution, they seem determined to persevere in the
work they have thus commenced. Our best wishes go with them, though we
ourselves are not in favor of turning the energies and resources of the Order in
that direction. Bro. Smith urges a more strict enforcement of the law relative
to gambling, profane swearinp; and intemperance, announces the issue of fourteen Dispensations for new Lodges, and concludes with a recommendation
that the Grand Lodge pay the expeuses of the Grand Officers in attending at its
Communications.

By-Laws and Permanent Resolutions of the Grand Lodge, many of them having become inoperative, and others requiring alteration ; and concludes by de·
clining to be a candidate for reelection.
The Report on Foreign Correspondence is again from the pen of Bro.
WILLIAM STORER, and when we remarked in one portion of it the expression of his "ardent desire to make this a short report," it was impossible to repress a feeling of the deepest sympathy with the gratification he must
have experienced at finding that he· had actually been enabled to compress it
within the brief space of ninety-four octavo pages, principally of brevier. Jesting aside, however, we do not quarrel with long reports, having to some extent
afflicted our own Grand Lodge in that respect ; and it is impossible not to ad·
mire the amount of labor bestowed, as well as the zeal and ability displayed by
Bro. STORER in this department of Masonic literature. He speaks in terms of
high commendation of the Address of the Grand Master of California in 1866,
and quotes largely from its pages. He is in favor of the proposition that all
Masons, whether members ot' the Lodge or not, should be permitted to vote in
any Lodge upon the question of admitting candidates ; and is a firm advocate
of the absolute righJ, to visit. The tlrst of these questions is rather a new one,
and as we can not perceive that any benefit to the Order would ensue from the
change of a custom almost universal, even did we wish such change, we shall
not pause to discuss it. The second, we have had occasion to express our opinions upon before, and the Grand Lodge of this State has agreed with Maryland
and Ohio in that respect. Bro. ST01i&n quotes largely from the proceedings of
Vermont in reference to the new" Grand Lodge of Canada,'' and offers a resolution recognizing thnt organization, which we perceive was not adopted by the
Grand Lodge. He is opposed to a regulation of' Kentucky which permits the
Lodges to elect representatives in the Grand Lodge, when the proper officers
can not attend, insisting that the Master and Wardens only can appoint proxies,
" for the very good reason," as he says, " that the Lodge is not a member of the
Grand Lodge, and therefore has no right to be a representative." We must
beg leave to differ with our learned brother of Connecticut in this respect.
Whether a Lodge has the right " to be a representative " or not, there can be
little doubt that it has a right to be represented. Grand Lodges at the present
day are in effect the Legislatures of .the Fraternity, and as the Masters and
Wardens are elected for the purpose, among other things, of representing their
respective Lodges in the Grand Lodge, if, from any cause, it becomes impossi-

KANSAS.
Another star has appeared In the Masonic firmament. Amid all the trouble11
which, during the past two or three yearH, have arisen In this Territory, it ap·
pears that " Freemasonry still survives; " a Grand Lodge having been established in this so lutely Indian country.
·
The first attempt at organlzafom was certainly I\ blunder, and from the subsequent action that appears to have been perceived. As early as November,
1855, "a meeting of delegates from several Masonic Lodges" was held at the
Town of Lea\•enworth, for the purpose of taking steps to form a Grand Lodge.
There were then three chartered Lodges in the Territory, from one of which
two representatives were pre@ent, and from another, one. The third Lodge be!ng absent, it ~as concluded to delay proceedings, and "the Convention adJOurued " until the twenty-seventh day of December following. On that day
the eame two Lodges only were again represented, each by a single officer, but,
singular to relate, these two Mastel'I! (with six other Masons present) proceeded
to orgnnize a Grand Lodge, to adopt a Constitution and code of By-Law~. and
to elect a full list of Grand Officers!
Refiection or better counsel seems to have come to their aid, however, and on
the seventeenth of March, 1856, "delegates from all the chartered Lodges" again
Msembled at Leavenworth, and reenacted all that which had been done before.
The same Constitution was adopted, and, with one exception, the same officers
were elected, - the Grand Master being installed by three Masters of Lodge&
HHing thns completed its organization in accordance with the rule which seem~
now to be an established one in the United States, we have great pleasure in
greeting this thirty-fonrth " addition to the family " - presenting our most
cordial wishes that the little mal-practice exhibited at its birth may not In any
wise prove detrimental to its health and growth. The M.·. W. •• RICHARD R. REES
was elected Grand Master, and the R.·. W.·. CHARLES F. HA1rarsoN, Grand Secretary.

tent. Dro. FosTER speak!! of the Indiana report of 1855 as being " sometimes

a Grand Lodge undertakes the distribution of charity, how unequal, uncertain
and infrequent must it be, especially in an extensh·e jurisdiction like Ohio. Un·
fair too, it is likely to be, as all the Lodges are ta..'l:ed to fill the treasury of the
Grand Lodge, and this money would be apportioned among a very few, living
probably in the neighborhood of the place where that body meets, and appropri·
ated without that certain knowledge of the worthiness of the applicants which a
subordinate Lodge would have the time and means to ascertain. It appears to
us to be far better that the revenue of the Grand Lodge, derived from its subor·
dinates, should be only just sufficient to meet its necessary business expenses, and
that to the Lodges should be left such disbursements as the calls for charity may
require and their means may justify. Bro. FosTER very justly condemns the proposition of the Grand Master of Oregon in 1855, to which we last year alluded,

in each case, it was represented that the Officer had not been able to discharge
the duties of his office, to a greater or less extent. The Grand Master is of course
a better judge than we, but it is difficult to conceive from the published proceedings that this system so far has been productive of any particular good in
N ew York. The theory is a good one, a nd could Deputies be found who would
always perform the duties proposed for them, fully and faithfully, it is impossible
to deny that ffi!Ch a system would be productive of most beneficial effocts ; as the
Lodges would by such means be subjected to a nearer and more scrutinizing
supervision. But our reading of the proceedings of the various Grand Lodges
for the past three y ears, preparatory to writin g our reports, haR shown us, in most
cases, how signally the practical eftects have failed to keep pace with the theoretical benefits. Year after year it bas been the same-a few only of the Deputies
making reports at all, and of those few, the greater portion making a report only
to show r easons why they have done little or nothing of that which was expected
from them. And thus, though strongly impressed· w ith the good results which
might be derived from such a system of sub-divided surveillance, nnd at one time
almost inclined to recommend it, we are admonished by the experience of other
jurisdictions that, as a general rule, it is impracticable to find a sufficient number
of those who will properly fulfill its dutieR, and that we must look to some other
mode for the accomplishment of the benefits it proposes.
We are not much in the habit of making up our reports with f!Cissors, but it
does sometimes happen that a brief, or even a lengthy abstract, cannot do justice
to a subject as presunted in the .proceedings of other jurisdictions. Believing the
case of the proffer ed mediation by the Grand Lodg e of Pennsylvania, between
the Grand Lodge of New York and the pretended, though outlawed body of that
name, to be one of these instanceR, and thinking it proper that the severe, though
just and well-merited rebuke which has been given to Pennsylvania for its 11rrogance and discourtesy, not more in the proffer than in the manner in which it wn~
made, should be presented in full, we give the following special report by the
Committee on Foreign Cor r espondence of New Y ork, to whom the subject had

"We remark one occurrence among the proceedings whic.h, with our limited knowledge
of the extent of Masonic powers and prerogatiYe~, seemed somewhat singular-the suspt11Sion of a Mason, for refusal to obey a summons, by the order of the Masttr of the
Lodge. And this act was approved by the Grand Lodge, although the offending Brother
was restored by its order. We had heretofore supposed that such power of punishment
resided in the Lodll"e alone, and was then properly exercised only after charges were
preferred and a fair trial offered.''

Although it was unnecessary to copy a great part of the foregoing, as a charge
or untruth, in eftcct, lies against us, we have thought it proper to give every word
of the report, so far as it relates to the case at ill8ue, without presuming to correct

It will be seen that the certainly not very offensive form of dissent therein
expressed was directed solely to the question of the right of a Master of a Lodge,
by his own will, and without action of his J,odge, to :mspend a Mason from all the
rights and privileges of the Order. It was our impresston at the time, that the
a.ct was in consequence of the refusnl of the party thus dealt with to obey a sum
mons, nnd we so recorded it. But thnt was a mere incident. It would 'not have
mattered to us whether that was the real cause, or whether he had stood on his
head in open Lodge, or whether, as it is now averred was the fact, he treated the
authority of the Master with contumely, so fnr as this mode of punishment was
concerned. Our simple opinion was that the Alaster had no right to assume s1icli
powers for any cause. That he might have caused the offending melllber to be led
out of the room, that he had the power to exclude him thereafter from the meetings
of the Lodge, (his proper exercise of such power being alwa,Ys subject to the ecru tiny
of a higher authority) we presume no one will doubt ; but mall our reading of the
works of many Masonic writers, and with a tolerable knowledge of the proceedings of those Grand LodgeR of the world with which this Grand Lodge is now in
correspondence, we do not remember that we ever heard before of a Ma~ter exercising the plenary power of suspension or expulsion. Now this was the "occurrence" which we noted, and the language in which it was mentioned could have
given offence only to those whose cerebral cuticle was exceedingly thin indeed.
Yet the Oregon Committee now declare that " no such occurrence as the one
alluded to has taken place within our jurisdiction," an<l this unqualified and
wholesale denial would naturally enough lead to the conclusion that no Ru~pen
sion in such a manner had therein been ordered. In answer to this we will only
quote, verbatim, literatim et punctuatim, from a page of the proceedings of that

showing that these constitute the recorded data by means of which we are to be
instructed in the "legitimate duty of a Committee on Foreign Correspondence."

SOUTH CAROLINA.
It is our misfortune ever to receive the proceedings of this Grand Lodge too
late to notice them until an extra year has passed by. Those now before us are
for 1855, comprising one Special and four Quarterly Meetings, and the Annual
Communication and Feast on the twenty-seventh day of December - the M.'. W.·.
ALFRED PmcE, Grand Master, presiding at each Communication, and the W.•.
ALBERT G. MACKEY, being Grand Secretary.
At the January meeting a resolution was adopted that the proceedings at the
late celebration of the Centennial Anniversary of the Grand Lodge of South Carolina be heremetically enclosed in a brass box, bearing an inscription that it was
not to be opened for one hundred years (from 1854); which box was to be placed
in a bank, or other secure place, and the proceedings of each year hereafter are to
allude to it and its place of deposit, that it may not during that long period be
forgotten. Thus the brethren of the Palmetto State will be enabled in after times
t:> see how their progenitors did things "a hundred years ago."
At the Quarterly Communication in December, Bro. A.G. MACKEY presented
his customary Report on Foreign Correspondence. He adheres to the doctrine
that neither the Master or Wardens of a Lodge can resign, inasmuch as at their
installation they "have solemnly promised to perform the duties of their respective offices for the time for which they have been elected." Suppose imperative
necessity required their removal from the scene of their labors to another part of
the world. Mnst their private interests be sacrificed for the purpose of literally
fulfilling that promise? Is not the general instruction that Masonic duties are
not to interfere with those which we owe to ourselves, our families, or our country,
an inferential qualification of such n. pledge? Bro. MACKEY urges the adoption of
a uniform code of By-Laws for the government of Lodges under dispensation,
and in this, as well as in his opinion that any member of a Lodge in good standing, who has paid up his dues, is entitled to withdraw, we aro happy to say that
the Grand Lodge of California agrees with him. He pays a well-<leserved compliment to Louisiana Relief Lodge, No. 1; and we hope in another year, that a similar organization within our own limits will have earned from him an equally favorable notice. A few very appropriate remarks are given to matters in New
York. He says, very correctly, that "the effect of the dissensions in that State
have been unintentionally ~xaggerated by the writers of, reports for some years
past,'' and that the results of these.dissensions are felt much more abroad than at
home. " The schismatic bodies,'' says he, " are rapidly dwindling in numbers and
respectability, while the strength and influence of the legal Grand Lodge are as
great among all true Masons there as in any other jurisdiction." And he is of
the opinion that the pseudo Masonii: bodies of the city owe their present puny
existence rather to the "notices and comments, denunciation and abuse which
they have received from other jurisdictions, than to any principle of vitality which
is inherent in themselves." He alludes to the new Canadian organization, with
the expression of the opinion that "it is not to be doubted that the Grand Lodges
of the United States will, with one accord, extend the right hand of fellowship
and recognition to this, their youngest sister." From a constructionist so strict,
and an expounder of the law so conservative, we are somewhat surprised to hear
this'; and we are inclined to the opinion that at the time he wrote he could hardly
have received full information on the subject.
The Annual Communication and Grand Feast occurred on the anniversary of
St. John the Evangelist. The financial reports show a revenue for the year of
$5254, an expenditure of $11104, and a balance on hand of $254. Sixty chartered
Lodges and ene under Dispensation now exist in South Carolina.. The Grand
M1.11ter and GTand t!.eeretary were both reelected.

joua:Nii. OF PROdl:EDINGS.

[May,

The Grand Lodges of Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Oregon, and Vermont, have
acknowledged the right of the new organization, and have recognized and wel·
corned it. In Maine, Ohio, and South Carolina, committees have reported in its favor•
but no action wa5 had by those Grand Lodges. The committ~e in Louisiana ap·
pears for it in one place, apd against it in anotl\er. The committee in Connecti·
cut reported in favor uf its acknowledgment, but the Grand Lodge refused the re·
cognition, as have also the Grand Lodges of Alabama, Missouri, New York~
Massachusetts, and Virginia. The opinion of Maryland is, beyond all doubt, ad·
verse, and Illinois, for the present, declines to take definite action in regarcl to it.
In Vermont alone, on the one hand, has any particular argument been published.
in support of this Masonic Declaration of Independence, and that is certainly a
very able one indeed. In New York and Massachusetts only, on the other hand,
have appeared any exhibition of reasons for opposition to it, and these to us seem
very weighty ones. In truth, comparatively inexperienced as we must confess
ourselves to be, we do not hesitate to say that when three such Grand Lodges as
those of Massachusetts, New York and Virginia unite in opinion upon a question
of such consequence, we should deem it presumptuous in ourselves to set up an
opposing one, even did we entertain it. But we do uot in this instance. Sincerely
as we sympathize with our Canadian brethren in thP.ir efforts for an. inde~enden~
organization, and gladly as we would welcome them to the fam1ly ot Grand
Lodges, could their entry be effected in a legitimate and Masonic manner, we
cannot feel it consonant with our duty to recommend their recognition now. The
able and judicious report presented to this Grand Lodge at the last Communica·
tion by the committee to whom the eloquent appeal of the "Grand Lodge of Can·
ada" was referred, met our hearty approbation ; and as we perceive by a commu·
nication received from the Provincial Grand Lodge of Canada West during the
past year, that the whole subject is now before the Grand Lodge of Er.gland, with
some prospect of a satisfactory termination, we shall suggest no other action than
that proposed last year by Bro. CuaT1s.

Secretary of Conrre11,

The peculiar interest which must necessarily attach to the 'proceedings of an
aHemblage of this kind, the first we have ever heard of, will prove a 1ufficient
justification, we trust, for giving to them so much space in this report. We had
not time, overborne as the writer of this has been with other busine11 of the Grand
Lodge, to prepare an abstract, and even had time been given, it is probable we
should have preferred to present them thus, as thereby the manner, as well u the
subltaace of the transactions is exhibited. With but little exception, the few re·
suits arrived at are precisely the conclusions which have e,·er governed Americaq
Masonry, so far as they extend, and the action of the Congress haa thu1 been complimentary to U9 of the Western Hemisphere. That Diplomas should be given
only to Ma1tP.r Masons, is the general, probably the universal practice in. the
United States; and that th~y should be in Latin and the language of the country
where issued, is the customary usage also. But the "testamentary formula" which
it is proposed they sho)lld contain, by virtue of which they are to be sent back to
the body whence they issued after the death of the holder, does not accord with the
practice in this country, nor with our views in regard to their uses. In America
such instruments are intended to be kept 9y the wives and children of the deceasc4
owner1, so that should neceslllty require 1t, they may be exhibited ns evidence•
of the right of those thus holding them to make claim upon the Order for assist•
ance; and further too, many of the Grand Lodges of the Union, our own among
the number, direct the issue of Diplomas for Masons, after deata, for the benefit of
their widows and orphans. Of the other propositions we have not time to speak.
The whole affair is interesting, but we are not enabled to perceive that much
practical good is likely to result from it.
Your committee have thus presented a reflex of the transactions of thirty·one
of the Grand J,odges of the United States, together with such informntion from
Foreign Grand Bodies as has been communicatAd by them. They have paused
but little to discuss or comment upon any subject, having been compelled to hasten
through this labor, almost with locomotive speed; and now, almost at the very hour
for your assembling, having performed this taPk entirely during the later hours of the
night, our pen is laid a~ide with the profoundest satisfaction, and its hurried production is presepted "with all its imperfections on it~ head."
All of which is respectfully submitted.
ALEX. G. ABELL,
Chairman Com. For. Corrtapondence.

To the M.-. W. •. Grand Lodge of California : Your committee, to whom was rpforred tho appeal of J. McD. Ros~, expelled
by Tuolumm Lodge, No. 8, March 21st, 1857, beg leave to report that they have
carefully examined the papers in tbut cn•e, and find the decision m:ide to be
solely and simply this: That inasmuch as the appellant received the three degree~ of MllSOnry without having paid thci.focs therefor, he is guilty of" ha\'lng
obtained money under f'nlsc pretences!" Sufficient testimony, in the opinion of
the. committee, is contained m the appeal papers, (to wit, that of the Worshipful
Master, presiding at the trial,) to show that in November, 1856. property was
placed in the hands of the first officer of the Lodge, by the appellant, sufficient
to fully meet all his indebtednes8 to that body ; from which it must be concluded
that there has been no c.lear disposition evinced to wrong the Lodge.
Your committee feel some regret at being compelled to differ from tho.a.ction
of this Lodge, when the names appearing would seem to pre-~upposo such mature judgment in Masonic jurisprudence. They do not consider it safe, howl'ver,
for the Grand Lodge to pursue a course which might seem.a protcciion of an of~

and they again urgently request further action at our hands upon this subJectaction which, to meet their l,lllplied desires, must be of 11 character totally different
from that had at our last Annual Communication, for their benefit. In fact, it is
complaiued that the conclusions then arrived at had the undesigned effect of rendering their difficulties still more intricate, rather than that of affording them relief. If this bas unhappily been the case. our brethren should attribute it more
to an over-zeal on their own part, which led them to represent their grievances in
a strong light to the Grand Lodge, than to inattention on the part of that body.
'fbe resolution adopted at the last Communicat ion was, in our opinion, a proper
l\nd necessary one ; and if the facts are as they then appeared to be from all the
information which the Grand Lodge bad in its possession, so far from repealing or
modifying that resolution we should rather feel called upon to require Hawaiian
Lodge to observe a, strict obedience to it, even if in so doing all those who have
hitherto shown themselves to be "good and true" should ~bandon them and
"worship at altars erected to ftilse Gods." No Mason should hold Masonic communication with any person until he is satisfied fully and beyond a doubt that
that person is 11 brother : nor should one Lodge commune with another until it
has assurance that that other bas been properly established and has a legal exist1mcc .; and a brother who visits a Lodge styling itself as one of Masons, without
ueing satisfied of its lawful authority to meet and work, does that which shows a
total disregard of those teachings which he received at the very threshold of our
lnsti tu tion.
Yct whilst we would by every guard preserve the fraternity within this jurisdiction from imposition, still would we be equally ca,reful that none who can establish
at claim to our fraternal consideration should in the slightest degree be. treated
with 11isrespect. With these views then, we would be most happy to know that
the organization styled " L e Progrla de l'Or.eani.e" WM really what it professes to
be, a legal Masonic organization under any jurisdiction recognized by us. That
pure and holy Masonic Hpirit which is ever to be found in a true Masonic Lodge,
induces J,odges properly established to afford not only to separate organizations
of known leipi.1 existence, evidence of its recognized authority to work, but even
deigns to s~tisfy a single member of th11t separate organization, should be desire
it. Now as our brethren of Jlawaiian Lodge ·have, or Hhould bll.ve been ever
ready to afford tc any nod all who desired it, the proofs of' their legal existence
ns a Lodge, so with that feeling or spirit of fraternal reciprocity which pervades
all l\fasouic intercourse, 'a similar favor should be extended to our brethren of'
Hawaiian Lodge by "Le Progrla de l'Oe«znic." It is clearly the duty of our liretbren of Jlawaiian Lodge to satisfy themselves of the legt\l existence of any alleged
Masonic body before the;1: enter its portals; and even had not the resolution of
last year been adopted, if a member of 11ny Lodge within this Jurisdiction should
knowingly sit iu a Lodge styled :Masonic, but not having .a legal existence, no
Mason could doulJt his unfitnes.~ to sit thereafter in a lawful Lodge. If then
l\Iasons-those who originally were entitled to all the benefits nnd privileges of
Masonry - in grasping at the shadow have lost the substance; if, in their great
desir e for clmnge and novelty they have forgotten their first lessons and have
attempted an organizatiQn without authoritr; and if, under these circumstances,
others will persist in r ecognizing and holdmg communication · with them, they
must suffer the consequences of their own willfulncBS, antl meet the penalty of
their disobedience to our laws.
If Le Progrla de L 'Oceanie possci;scs the proofs of her legal existence and does
not afford them to visitors or neighboring Lodges, the prganizatio)l is undeserving
of 11ny courtesy or consideration at our bands. If there be no such proofs, the
self-styled Lodge is unlawful1 and must of course receive our condemnation.
What we have said of the proofs of a legal existence we wish to be understood
ns meaning the proofs that there was an emanation from a Masonic organization
of known und recognized authority ; an adherence to that authority; and a continued, constant, and unceasing existence both in the supreme and subordinat e
organizations. So if Le Progrls de L'Owinie has not these proofs, our brethren of
Hawaiian Lodge must discard her and her misguided members.
Steps have lJeen taken by our R:. W.·. Grand Secretary to ascertain from France
the facts in regard to the Lodge Le Progrb de L' Oe«znie, ancl until we are fully in·

the following report : 1b the M:. W.·. Grand Lodge of Oalif(Yf'nia:Your committee, to whom were referred the By-Laws of the Subordinate Lodges, have had the same under consideration, and beg leave to report, that they
have carefully examined all those submitted to them, and approve them, with
the exception of those named below-in which they recommend the following
nmendments : Tuolumne Lodge, No. 8.-To so amend Art. V., that it may conform to the 42d
Standing Resolution of the Grand Lodge; and, at the request of the Lodge, to so
amend Art. VI., as to fix the fees for the degrees at thirty, twenty, and twentyfive dollars, respectively.
Mo/Clllumne Lodge, No. 31.-To so amend Article VIII., at the request of the
Lodge, as to fix the monthly dues at one dollar.
St. John's Lodge, No. 37.-To amend Sec. 1, of Art. II., at the request of the
Lodge, by striking out the word "November," and inserting the word "September;" to so amend Seo. 1, of Art. 4, that it may conform to Sec. 1, of Art. X, of
the Constitution ; and to amend Sec. 2, of Art. IV., at the request of the Lodge,
by striking out the word " six," and inserting the word " three."
SafJT'amento Lodge, No. 40.-To f>O amend Article I., that it may conform to the
40th Standing Resolution of the Grand Lodge.
Los Angeles Lodge, No. 42.-Tci' J3trike out Secs. 10 and 21, of Art. II., which
are deemed improper.
Rough and &ady Lodge, No. 52.-To strike out Art. XII., as it conflicts with
the established Regulations for Trials.
Union Lodge, No. 58.-To reduce the affiliation fee, at the request of the Lodge,
from ten to five dollars.
Natuma Lodge, No. 64.-To so amend Sec. 1, of Art. II., that it may conform to
Sec. 1, Art. X., of the Constitution ; and to append the following worcls to Art XL :
" subject to the approval of. the Grand Lodge."
Quitman Lodge, No. 88.-To strike out Art. XII, as it conflicts with the es~ab­
lished Regulations for Trials.
Your committee would recommend that St. James Lodge, No. 54; Enterpri11
Lodge, No. 70 ; Mount Zion Lodge, U. D. t and St. Mark'a Lodge, U. D., be instructed to adopt the Uniform Code of By-Laws, aR recommended by the Grand
Lodge at its last Communication, instead of those they now present, which contain many objectionable features. Your committee are gratified to find that full
three fourths of the Lodges under this jurisdiction have already adopted said
Code.

THE STANDING RESOLUTIONS.

'l'he JDth aml 50th Standing' Uesolutions were so amemle1l as to read as fol·

lows:49. Resolved, That the right (so called) to visit Masonically, is not an a.b•olme ri;rht,
but is a favor which every lawful Mason in good standinir is entitled to ask, and wnich
Lodge should refuse unless good and sufficient objection to such admission is made
hy a regular member; in which case the Master, in his discretion, may admit or exclude
the visitor.
50. Resolved, That this Grand Lodge having recognized the principle that no one
•hall be initiated into the mysteries of our Order, except in the Lodge nearest his place of
residence (unless t>y the proper permission); and having, by an established regulation,
tnken care to avoid infringing the jurisdictional right$ of others, will not tolerate that its
own be invaded; and it is tlierefore ordered that no Lodge subordinate to the Grand
l,odgc of California, shall admit to membership any person who, being at the time a re·
Rident of this State, bas received, or chims to have received the degrees of Masonry
from any sourr.e beyond the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge, without proper permission
from the Lodge nearest his plaee of residence, until he shall have paid into the hands of
the Secretary of the Lodge to which he applies for membership, the full amount charged
by that Lodge for conferring the degrees, less the sum paid by him to the Lodge in winch
he received them.
110

The following additional resolution was adopted : 71. Resolved, That the subordinate Lodges be required to instruct one of their repre•
•entatives hereafter to remain in attendance upon the Grand Lodge until the close of its
Communications.

SECTION I. The Grand Lodge is the Supreme Masonic Power and Authority
In this State, possessing all the attributes of sovereignty and government, legislative, executive, and judicial, - limited only by a strict adherence to the
Ancient Landmarks of the Order, and to 'the provisions of its own Constitution
and Regulations.
SEc. 2. Its Legislative powers extend to every case of legislation, not expressly delegated by itself to the Lodges ; and the Constitutions and Regulations,
which it has an inalienable right to adopt and promulgate at its own convenience, and to alter, amend, or repeal at its own pleasure, under the limitations
therein imposed, are final and binding upon all Lodges and Masons within its
,
jurisdiction, until so ~ltered or repealed by its own act.
SEc. 3. Its Executive powers include the granting of' Dispensations and Charters
to all Lodp;t18 within this State, and to Lodges in other territory where no Grand
Lodge exists ; the revocation or suspension thereof; the issuing of special
11iApensat.ions for all purposes permitted by any of the provisions of this ConAtitution ; and the exercise, generally, of e.ll snch authority as may be necessary
to carry its own legislation into complete effect.
SEc. 4. Its Judicial powers are of two kinds; 1st - Original - Including the
decision of nll controversies between any of the Lodges, or between one of them
1111d a member or members of another, or between members of different Lodges ;
nnd the enforcement of discipline upon its own members and upon the Lodges
under its jurisdiction ; and 2d -- Appellate - Embracing the revision of all
matters of contfoversy or discipline, proper for Me.sonic investigation, which
may have fLrisen in any of the Lodges, and over which it has not retained original jurisdiction.

SEC. 4. The Past Ma~ters of each Lodge, collectively, shall be entitled to one

SEC. 5. No Grand Officer, Past Grand Officer, or Past Master, voting or participating in a vote in either of those capacities, shall vote or participate in a
vote in any other of them; but either of such members may, as Master, Warden,
or representative of a Lodge, cast also the vote or votes to which sueh position
shall entitle him.
SEC. 6. When a Lodge shall be fully represented by its Master and Wardens,
and shall be entitled only to three votes, each of those officers may cast one vote.
SEC. 7. When a Lodge shall be fully represented by its Master and Wardens,
~nd shall be entitled to more than three votes, the additional vote or votes may
he cast by those officers in the order of their rank; as thus- if the Lodge have
foar votes, the Master may cast two; if it have five, the Senior Warden may
also cast two; if six, the Junior Wnrden may also cast two; and thus again for
any number of votes to which the Lodge may be entitled.
. SEC. 8. When a Lodge shall be represented by only two of its proper officer!!,
if the number of votes to which it is entitled be even, each officer m1Ly cast an
equal number ; if odd, the officer highest in rank may cast the odd vote.
SEc. 9. When a Lodge shall be represented by only one of. its proper officers,
or by a representative, such officer or repre11entative may cast nil the votes to
which it is entitled.
S11:c. 1O. In all cases of IL tie vote, except votes by ballot, the Grand Master,
in addition to his proper vote, may have the casting vote.

be by name especially exempted from such effect.

as provided in Sec. 5, Art. VIII., Purt J.

Of Amendments, Definitions and Forms.
ARTICLE I.
OF AMENDMENTS.
SECTIOS 1. Any proposed amendmrnt to this Constitution shall be presented at
nn Annual Communication, and shall in all cases be referred to the Committee
on Jurisprudence, who shall report before a vote thereon be taken.
.
S:sc. 2. After the report of the committee, if the vote in favor of such proposed
amendment be unanimous, it shall be declared adopted, and from and after the
cloEe of that Communication, shall become a p11rt of the Constitution.
SEC. 3. If the vote in favor of such proposed amendment be not unanimous,
lmt there be a majoritr therefor, it shall lie over for one year, and shall be published with the proceedmgs under the caption of " Proposed Amendments to the
Constitution;" and at the next succeeding Annual Communication. if it shall
receive a majority of the votes given thereon, it shall be declared adopted, and
from and after the close of that Communication, shall become n part of the Constitution.
SEC. 4. No vote upon 11 proposed amendment shall be taken after the election
of the Grand Officers.
SEC. 5. All former written Constitutions of this Grand Lodge are hereby repealed, as are aho all Regulations, or parts thereof, which are repugnant to or
JDconsistent with this Constitution ; and no Regulation shall hereafter be adopted which shall be in violation of or inconsistent with any of its provisions.

The foregoing report was received and concurred in, nod the
brethren therein named were admitted to seats.
The reading of the proceedings at the last Annual Communication
was dispensed with, the members being furnished with printed copies
thereof.
The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to the Grand
Lodge of California, as follows : BRETHREN OF THE MOST WORSHIPFUL
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA:

ONCE more in the passage of time we are permitted to meet in our annual c~n­
vocation to consult in regard to the interests of our beloved Order, and to devise
those means best adapted to its continuance and prosperity, to insure its
permanency, and to develope its inner life, that its good may be felt where~er
its name is known, and that those who are around us, and to whom each action
of the Fraternity becomes a thing of closest scrutiny, may acknowledge and
approve our course, as one claiming the sympathy of the good, the assistance
of the benevolent, and the earnest prayers of all who ~ould aid the friend
of the friendless-the guardian of the fatherless and destitute.
.
To that Divine Master of us all, whose eye overlooks a11, and whose kmd
providence guards the path which each of us does tread, our most humble and
heartfelt thanks for our preservation and return to this ball in peace are due.
J greet you here to-day, my brethren, and it is with great joy that I see so
many present whom I have met in preceding years, interchanging thoughts,
comparing work, and toiling together for the common good of the Craft.
And yet this joy which I feel at beholding so many here that I have met before,
hath its shade of sadness. Mortality has claimed its tribute from among us.
There are places here we were wont in times gone by, to see filled by familiar
faces, which will be seen no more; voices, once heitrd with pleasure, are forever hushed in the deep silence of the grave ; and forms that moved among
us the personation of all that was manly and worthy of being loved, have crumbl~d to their p~rent dust. Noble spirits have-burst the bands that bound them.
here, to enter the untried future. Gentle souls have escaped the sorrows of
earth and time, to seek the fruition of their hearts' hopes in heaven and eternity-each carrying with him a record of his work for the inspection of the
Infinite.
Ours is not a legislature of political sovereignty, or of social rights or conduct that is to govern men in their political or social intercourse purely, but a
higher one-one that ministers to the sick heart and desponding mind. The
one can be reversed, and a succeeding enactment of sovereignty may amend
and restore rights taken and repair wrongs done. Not so our legislation, whirh
is but the interpretation of principles having with them the sanction of centuturies the adhesion of the great of the past, and the earnest support of the
emine~t of the present. One wound inflicted upon that ancient structure mars
the fairness of its proportions, and is attended by consequences of so great a
magnitude that the most reckless should shrink from their contemplation with
dismay. It is a loosened joint which will be fo11owed by the decay that precedes the fall of the temple. Those ancient land-marks once attacked and

weakened, ijO succeeding convocation can restore to them their strength and
beauty.
It is a source of satisfaction that I am able to congratulate you at this time
upon the general welfare and prosperity of our beloved Order in this Commonwealth. With a firm and steady, though silent exercise of its powers, it has
extended its numbers, widened its field of usefulness, and exemplified its principles-endearing its members to t he precepts which govern it, and knitting
with closer ties each to the other in the sustaining of the rights so dear to all;
while without our circ.le of brotherhood, the world has been taught to resp~ct
our motives, and appro ve our actions.
This general harmony of action and feeling has met with but one interruption which has come to my knowledge, and that.is in the instance of Lebanon
Lodge, No. 49. One of its members having been guilty of a gross violation of
Masonic law and duty, and the Lodge having refused to punish him therefor,
believing it to be for the best interests of the Fraternity, I arrested the Charter
of that Lodge, suspended the offending member from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, and summoned him to appear and take his trial before this
Grand Lodge. All the papers in reference to this case are in. the hands of the
Grand Secretary.
To the wise, this general prosperity presents its elements of danger-for
while there is nothing seemingly to guard against, a relaxation of that vigilance
which should always watch at the portals of .our temple., is most to be dreaded.
This is true in all lands and among all societies. How much more forcibly
may it be put in this land of strangers, coming from every country, speaking evory
tongue, the representatives of every people. Unknown t o each other, save in
that restless and careless association which marks the society of the people of
this great and growing Commonwealth; their past history beyond our knowledge; their hearts a sealed book which we have no power to open or peruseall should be subject to the closest scrutiny, and if aught is found upon which
to base the slightest doubt, it should make an impassable barrier between them
nnd us. It is far better that we turn away many good men from our altars,
than that we hazard oar good no.me and reputation by accepthig a single bad
one; for upon that reputation rests, in an eminent degree, our power to do
good. I have every reason to believe that the fraternity in this State are both
zealous and vigilant in the discharge of their duties in this respect. The
course now pursued by the Subordinate Lodges is such as necessarily impresses
the work upon each one who receives it, and forms the foundation p.pon which
to build a complete masonic education. The t horough examination to which
the candidates are subjected as they progress, renders it impossible that any
should be ignorant of the principles ta~ght or the duties enjoined by our
venerable and benevolent Institution.
Considering the circumstances which have governed the establishment of the
Order in this State, the harmony-attained in working is a source of congratulation to all. This was scarcely to have been expected, and it speaks volumes
for the earnestness and faithfulness of those who have contributed to such a
result. I would recommend that the work heretofore sanctioned by this
Grand Lodge, be fully exemplified at this Communication.
In obedience to a resolution of the Grand Lodge, I visited San Francuco
Lodge, No. 7, in May last, and am happy to state that the differences then existing in that Lodge have been amicably settled, and t hat peace and harmony
have fully been restored.
Many applications for d,ispensations have been made t o me for t he purpose
of conferring the degrees upon applicants in less time than that provided by
the Constitution, because the candidates were about leaving the Stat e. These [
have inyariably refused, for the reason that t hose applying had been living
within a short distance of Lodges for years, and had never discovered that
they could be of benefit to the Fraternity until they learned that t he Fraternity
could be of immediate benefit to them; and for the further reason, that I do
not think we have any right to inflict upon our brethren eleswhere half

the one legally existing. Th~ act is in direct violation of all Masonic law, and we
cannot recognize those as just and true members of our Fraternity who could
so far forget its teachings as to mar by such high handed measures its peace
and harmony. Your early attention is invited to this subject, as containing:
that which is of vital importance to the well-being of the Craft. They
ask a recognition at your hands. Schism may be easily crushed in its infancy,
which, left to grow, might defy our utmost power.
I have received and herewith submit to you, a circular issued by authority
of the Grand Lodge of the State of Maine, containing a resolution urging the
formation of a General Grand Lodge of the United Stittes, to meet in September, 1859. The high Masonic source from which this emanates renders it deserving of your respectful consideration. The reasons urged by the committee are
forcibly and cogently stated, and are undoubtedly the result of a pure desire
to contribute to the welfare of the Order, as well as to perfect it in harmonious
action. l therefore present it to you for such action as you may deem best
calculated to promote the general good of our Institution.
I have also rece.iyed, and herewith submit for your consideration, certain
resolutions of the Grand Lodge of Virginia, asking t he cooperation of the
Grand Lodge of California in raising funds fo r the purchase of Mount Vernon.
There are none whose pride and patriotism, as well as fraternal love and respect, will not be awakened on a subject so dear to the Masonic heart. Our
reverence for the past, our thankfulness for tho blessings which throng t he
present, our hopes of the future, and our gratitude to the memory of the illustrious dead, all prompt us to every exertion to become the possessors of the
place where repose the remains of our brother and chief, GEORGE WASHINGTON;
making his tomb-as in time it must be-the Mecca of the patriot's pilgrimage.
The continuance of the difficultie~ which still surround and embarr11ss our
brethren of Hawaiian Lodge, No. 21, in the Hawaiian Islands, demands careful
consideration at your hands, that some means be adopted t o relieve t hem from
the annoyances which constantly disturb their harmony and peace, in consequence of the existence of tfie so-called Lodge Le Progria de l' Oceanie, at
that place.
You will be called upon at this Communication to determine upon a change
in the organic law of Masonry in this State. You'can not exercise too much
care and wisdom in the enactment or a.Iteration of the laws which are so vitally to affect the Fraternity. Too much legislation is ever attended with a
danger of encroaching upon the ancient landmarks of the Order, or infringing
upon some of those rights which are the inalienable inheritanye of each member, however humble.
I would respectfully recommend a thorough revision of the Standing Resolutions, as many of them are inoperative, and as the reasons which gave rise to
others ha.ve ceased to exist, leaving some useless, and others Injurious in their
operation. The substance of many of them is embodied in the proposed new
Constitution which was presented at your la.~t Communication, and which you
will have to pass upon at this. A few clear and concise regulations are all
that are needful, and would fulfil their office much better t han the many without that conciseness. I would also recominend a repeal of the resolution permitting the subordinate Lodges to ballot for the three degrees at the so.mo
time. If not an infringement upon Masonic usage, as I am in,clined to think it
is, it he.a been, and I think must ever be, attended with confusion and evil t o
the Fraternity. There are too few guards around us to dispense with any one
of them. They were framed with long thought, have endured the lapse of
time unshaken, and have.survived the world's frown and condemn11tion. They
exert now, and always have exerted a salutary effect upon the Order, and I
think we had better leave them as our Masonic fathers projected and transmitted them to us. It is a source of pain to me to see the desire for change
and alteration which has invaded our councils, as the preservation of our
marks of antiquity alone gives to us the benefit of that universality which is
one of our greatest boasts. Once admitted to change, and every link which

During my term of office I have issued Dispensations for the establishment
of ten new Lodges, the names and 109ations of which will be found in the report of the Grand Secretary. They are all in good working condition, and
their members appear zealous and competent to perform all the duties enjoined
by the laws of the Craft. I recommend a careful examination of their work,
and if it meets the approbation of the Grand Lodge, that Charters be granted
·
them.
The difficulties which nt one time threatened the harmony of Iowa Hill
Lodge, No. 63, and Wisconsin Hill Lodge, No. 74, have been settled, both having surrendered their Charters, and a portion of the members of both having
consolidated under a new Dispensation, with the name of Ionic Lodge.
The Dispensation under which Folsom Lodge was working has been given
up, and its members have affiliated with Natoma Lodge, No. 64, to which I
granted a dispensatior. to change its location from Mormon Island to the town
of Folsom-a place better adapted to sustain the Lodge in its course of use, fulness.
Upon petition from the members of Humboldt Lodge, No. 79, for a dispensation to remove their Lodge from Bucksport to Eureka, as being a place more
convenient for them, and better enabled to support the Lodge, I have granted
their request, and the Lodge is now working at the last named place.
Invited by the German Benevolent Society of San Francisco, with the assistance of the members of the Grand Lodge I laid the corner-stone of the
German Hospital in that city, iu accordance with ancient Masonic usage. The
kindness and consideration with which the Fraternity were treated on that
occasion, was strong evidence of the good repute in which it is held by those
without its membership. The prejudice which once trammeled its action is
fast sinking before its tread, and the hands and hearts of the good and true on
all sides are found cheerfully contributing to our prosperity and fEJ.me.
The Masonic Board of Relief, established something more than two years
ago by the several Lodges of the City of San Francisco, under a thorough
organization to administer to the distresses of those who are worthy and
needy, deserves our highest commendation for its active and efficient benevolence. The want of time, the cares of business, and the whirl of- pleasure,
often closes the hand which else would have been freely and cheer~ully opened
to minister to the wants of the destitute l\nd the unfortunate. In this board
of relief our brethren of San Francisco have avoided all those difficulties, RS
it is their business as well as plea.sure to give ear to all that apply, and as they
have full power to contribute to their needs and supply all their wants. The
great good which our San Francisco brethren have thus already done, is but
the guaranty for the boundless good for which the future will bless them.
Beyond the difficulties hereinbefore mentioned, our foreign intercourse, as
will appear by the report of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence, gives
a flattering exhibit of the harmony and prosperity of the 'Fraternity throughout the world. There has been no time in the history of Masonry when so
great an influence has been felt, or so large an amount of usefulness exhibited,
as at the present time. The shackles with which prejudice and ignorance have
hitherto bound it, unnerving, in a manner, its arm for extended good, and circumscribing its theatre of action, seem to have fallen at its feet ; nnd with
strength and vigor it is pressing forward in its path of duty to humanitywidening as human intelligence widens - spreadi'ng hand in hand with those
sciences which confer blessings upon mankind- and preparing tbe heart and
mind for a more noble appreciation of the sublimity of that justice and benevolence which it is confidently hoped will one day bind together the whole
' human family with indissoluble ties of friendship and affection.
Our Order, grand in its numbers and influence, will play a noble part in
this great scheme of universal brotherhood ; interpreting all languages, ac-

'
Our own Commonwealth, by the force of circumstances seems to have been

appended.

Since the books were balanced, and the foregoing accounts prepared, Wa,,hington, San Diego, Volca110, Live Oak, Humboldt, and .folar Star Lodges have
paid up the balances respectively to their debit, amounting in all to $250 50 ;
and there has been received from Iowa Hill Lodge the sum of $92 60, being
the net amount thus far realized, after payment of its debts, from the collection of its dues and the sale of its effects. Before the close of the Communication, the usual supplementary account of all moneys received since the fourth
day of March last will be presented for examination, though it will as heretofore form a part of the report of the following year .
In conclusion, the undersigned expresses the pleasure he feels in announcing that every Lodge under t he jurisdiction transmitted full returns for the
year 1857, and that the three which were delinquent at the time of publication
the year before, soon after remedied the fault. The creditable manner in
which nearly all those papers are prepared by the various Secretaries, should
not escape the attention of the Committee on Returns. A great and constant
