During the past three years the undersigned has exerted every effort to procure a complete series of the published transactions of the various American
Grand Lodges, as far back as they were to be found consecutively in print ·
and he takes this occasion to acknowledge the courtesy of the several Grand
Secretaries who have enabled him thus far to present the thirty-three large
volumes of valuable Masonic history above enumerated. A great number of
incomplete series of such proceedings still remain unbound, but it is believed
that during the ensuing year, most of the missing publications, as far be.ck as
the average of those now given, will be received, and it is probable that fifteen
or twenty more similar volumes can be presented at the next Communication.
As an earnest of our own willingness to reciprocate the courtesies here acknowledged and hoped for, the undersigned, in October le.st, transmitted to the
Grand Secretary of each Grand Lodge in the United States, and to severe.I foreign Grand Bodies, a copy of the republication of the proceedings of this Grand
Lodge from 1850 to 1854, inclusive, as prepared by him under the resolution
adopted in May, 1856.
By reference to the report on the Library me.de in 1855 1 it will be seen that
there were then but seventy-three volumes (excluding duplicates) in our possession. That number is now more than doubled, and it is the hope, as it
will be the constant effort of the undersigned, to make our collection of Masonic works, within a few years, the largest and most valuable on the Western
Continent. Among other books received during the past year, 11.re the thirty
volumes of Bro. RosERT MORRIS' valuable publication-the Universal Masonic
Library-which, though including many works already in the possession of the
Grand Lodge, yet contains many of importance not previously upon our
shelves. Two sets of this work were purchased, as ordered by the Grand
Lodge, but tho undersigned, knowing of no use for duplicates in the library
has disposed of one for the cost and expenses, as will appear in the fine.nciai
report of the Grand Secretary. It is strongly recommended as a most valuable
collection of' the writings of many of the best Masonic authors, which every
Lodge in the State ought to possess. A complete set of the " Me.sonic Review" has been obtained; the additional volumes of the" Freemason's Monthly
Magazine" have been bound, as have also sundry volumes of the " Temple,"
the "Masonic Union," and the " Signet and Journal" ; and severe.I other books
have been added, as will be seen in the foregoing cat11.logue.
For the disbursements made on these occasions, reference is me.de to the
orders upon the Grand Treasurer and his report; and it is recommended to
the Grand Loffge that a further appropriation be me.de for additions to the
Library during the coming year.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
ALEX. G. ABELL, Grand Secretary.

1b the Lodgea in the City of San Francisco :The Masonic Board of Relief of the City of San Francisco submits this, its
second Annual Report, to the constituent Lodges of which it is the represent.a..
tive with the hope that the manner in which the duties for which it was created
hav~ been discharged during the past year, may meet the approbation of those
whose charitable foresight called it into existence. In the compact between the
Lodges which established this Board, it was provided that semi-annual r~rts •
should be made to them, and during the year 1856, this requisition was complied
with.. The absolute inability, however, on the part of the officers of the Board,
to give the time necessary for the preparation of the lengthy statistical tables
which accompany this report, and which are required by the languag~ of the
compact, twice within the year, prevented the appearance of a rep?rt m July:
and it is now respectfully suggested th~t for all use.ful purposes a full and detailed report at the close of each year is amply sufficient.
With this day terminates the second year of the existence of the .Board of
Relief and had there been any doubts in the beginning in regard to the utility of
such ~n organization, all would now be dissipated by the practical results which
two years' experience of its beneficial workings have presented. At the date of
the last Annual Report six Lodges, viz.: California, No. l,Parfaite Union, No. 17,
Occidental, No. 22, Golden Gate, No, 30, ¥uunt Moriah, No. 44, and Lebanoo, No. 49,
were parties to the compact. Two others have since been added, while the last
named ho.s ceased its membership, its Charter having been arrested by the Grand
Master on the twenty-ninth day of June lo.st. At the commencement ~f .the
present year San Francisco Lodge, N.o. !, became a member o~ the Assoc1atio.n,
and on the sixth day of August, Fidelity Lodge, U. D., gave its o.ssent to the
compac.t : these, with those before na,!11ed, comprising all the Lodges in the city.

Bro. J AS. L . ENGLISH, from the committee t o whom was referred
the Grand Master's Address, presented the followi~g report: To the .M. •. lV. ·. Grand Lodge of California:Your committee to whom was referred the Address of the .M.·. l-V.·. Grand
blaster, have had the same under consideration and recommend the following
disposition of such portions thereof as require the action of this Grand Lodge:
We recommend that so much of said Address as refers to the refusal of
the Grand Master to grant dispensations for the conferring the degrees
upon applicants in less time than that provided by the Constitution; to his
refusal to grant dispensations to re-ballot for persons rejected, within the time
prescribed by the Constitution; to the circular issued by authority of tho
Grand Lodge of the State of Maine containing a resolution urging the formation of a General Grand Lodge of the United· States to meet in September,
1859; to the continuance of the difficulties which still surround and embarrass
our brethren of Hawaiian Lodge, No. 21; to a thorough revision of the Standing Resolutions; and to a repeal of the resolution permitting the subordinate
Lodges to ballot for the three degrees at the same t ime, be referred to the
Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence :
That so much of said Address as refers to the work of the subordinate
Lodges, and recommends that t he work heretofore sanctioned by this Grand
Lodge be fully exemplified at this Communication, be referred to the Committee on Work.:
That so much of said Address as refers to the issuing of Dispensations to
new Lodges, and recommends that Charters be granted them, be referred to
the Committee on Dispensations and Charters :
That so much of said Address as refers to the arrest of the Charter of
L ebanon Lodge, No. 49 ; to the suspension of an offending member of said
Lodge from all the rlghte and privileges of Masonry ; and to his being summoned to appear ·and take his trial before this Grand Lodge, be referred to a
special committee of five :
That so much of said Address as refers to the communication from the
Grand Orient of .France, expressive of its wish to establish more intimate relations with this Grand Lodge, be referred to _J special committee of three :
That so much of said Address as refers to the communication from the
Lodge "Clemente Amitie," at Paris, in France, soliciting aid in the benevolent
undertaking, by them begun, of establishing an Orphan Asylum, be referred
to a special committee of three :
That so much of said Address as refers to the Grand Lodge of Virginia,
asking the co-operation of the Grand Lodge of California in raising funds for
the purchase of Mount Vernon, be referred to a special committee of three:
And that so much of said Address as refers to the communication from the
Grand Master of Masons in Peru, giving information of the insubordination and

expulsio11 l'>y the Grand Orient of that Republic, of two Lodges under its jurisdiction, for unmasonic conduct; to the address from the seceding Lodges, announcing the establishment of an organization independent of the Grand
Orient of Peru ; and to the pamphlet containing their defence for so doing ; be
referred to the Committee on Foreign Correspondence, with instructions to
ascertain all the facts connected with or b~aring upon the subject, and to report at the next Communication of this Grand Lodge.
Your Committee approve of the action of the .Grand Master in issuing,
immediately upon the receipt of the communication from the Grand Master
of Peru, notices to the Lodges within the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge,
acquainting them with the facts, and prohibiting any intercourse with the rebellious Lodges or their members. No matter what the circumstances may
have been which led to the insubordination, he could not have acted otherwise,
consistently with Masonic law, until · the facts had been investigated by the
Prand Lodge, and other action recommended.
Your committee t(l.ke p-eat pleasure in saying that they regard the Address
itself as a model, and commend it to the careful attention and consideration
of the Brethren.
All of which is respectfully submitted.

He expresses bis surprise at a passing remark of ours In regard to sundry. strictures of other committees upon the practice of "going into Committee of' the
Whole" in the Grand Lodgt' of Indiana,-which was to the effect t.bat we saw
no reason why the brethren in that State should not be permitted to do their
own legislation in their own way t and he adds that mortification was felt, to1>,
at meeting " such an argument addressed to the consideration of experienced,
discriminating Masons, upon a subject of Masonic custom and usage,'' by those
· whom he considers as" intelligent." Now we think that Bro. BROWN will Bell,
upon reflection, that in this we offered no " argument" at all, and no opinion
even upon " a subject of Masonic custom and usage,'' for that implies something which is common to and affects the whole Craft. It was a mere suggestion that a little peculiarity In the domestic management of the Grand Lodge of
Indiana, was hardly a matter of sufficient importance to the Fraternity bejond
that jurisdiction, to make it worth while to wage war upon it; and we were induced to make the remark, because, in other instances besides this, as we then
said, "there is too frequent a disposition to find fault with the mere local practices or rep;ulations of' other bodies, for no better reason, generally, than that
they differ from those of the bodies to which the writers themselves belong."
It was not while treating of Florida that this paragraph was written, and we
did not then, and do not now intend it in the least to apply to her committee.
Nor did we, or do we, propose at all to defend or recommend the practice spoken
of. Nothing of the' kind occurs in the Grand Lodge of California, nor with our
assent ever would occur there. But our brethren of Indiana have thought differently, and as it appeared to us to be one of those things which concerned
themselves alone, we were not disposed to see them quaneled with in consequence, and were content to do what we have now done in nearly half 11 page
-say nothing at all aboµt it.

nullity :-That in case of a vacancy in the Mastership of a Lodge, that office
devolves upon the Senior Warden, and if he declines to preside, from any cause,
it is the duty (and right) of the Junior Warden to do so, even though the Senior
Warden be present :-That a member of n Lodge who foels himself agp;rieved by
a decision of the Master, must seek bis remedy by application to the Grand
Lodge ; and that it is the duty of a Master, upon proper request, to convene .b is
Lodge and attend the remains of a brother to the grave, "no matter what his
religious belief In life may have been ;" the only proper subject for inquiry
being whether he was in good standing In Masonry at the time of his decease.
All these accord with our own opinions.
The Report on Foreign Correspondence is presented by Bro. SAMUEI. LAW·
REKCE, the editor of the "Masonic Signet and Journal." In bis views regarding the rights' of Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts to be considertd as

organic laws, as would do away with that present generally acknowledged doctrine of the supremacy of Grand Masters, which had its origin probably during
the same period that gave birth to the equally sensible proposition that "the
King can do no wrong." We sha.ll not be alone in this heresy, for some of the
most eminent Masons in the Union have lat11ly and successfully advanced it in
those elevated and intellig~nt bodies, the General Grand Chapter and the Grand
Encampment of the Unit'ld States. As to the " protest,'' the Grand Master of
Illinois was right in the refusal to receive it. It is one of our promises to abide
by the decision of a majority of our brethren, and such a paper was in spirit a
violation of that promise, as it sought to record an unwillingness to submit to
the arbitrament, not of the Grand Master only, but of a large majority of the
members of the Grand Lodge.

amendment of the Constitution, making it requisite that the ]\faster of a Lodp;e
should have previously served as a Warden. This, Bro. DossoN thinks "the
strongest argument he had seen on that side" of the proposition, but it was not
sufficiently powerful to convince him, nor did it last its writer quite up to tb'e
next succeeding Communication of this Grand Lodge. Our own ideas upon this
subject, however, have been expressed in some one of our previous reports, and
we have little to add now beyond the fact that they were, and are consonant with
the action.of the Grand Lodge of this State. Without pausing to enquire into
the fact whether the "old Charges " of 1722, are entitled, as our brother of
Louisiana declares, to more reverence than the " old Regulations " of 1721, we
admit that we look upon them both as the law, so far as they are not manifestly
and palpably inconsistent with the well-being and necessities of the Order at the·
present day ; and it should be no light reason which would induce us to suggest
a departure from any plain and unmistakable direction contained in either. In
this case, however, were the" Charge" as absolute and distinct us Bro. DossoN
thinks it, (even' with an erroneous definition which be has given to one passage),
we have no doubt that a departure from it is perfectly justifiable, and for this
reason: That as the ''Old Charges" were given and received as the laws best
adapted for the government and prosperity of the Fraternity at the time when
they were promulgated, and were intended to operate as useful adjuncts to its success and perpetuity, so now, when a c,entury or•more has produced great changes
in the state of society which made some of those regulations useful and necessary, we may well and rightfully enquire whether an alteration of them in some
instances is not calculated to carry out the good results which were the sole
intent of the original law. When those" Charges" were written there is little
doubt that one who " had acted as a Wanlen" was likely to be the most competent person to ser ve as Master, and the good of the Order was evidently conaulted in the regulation. ls' it necessarily so now? On the contrary, does not
all our experience show that there are frequently those in a Lodge much better
qualified for the Chair than the brethren whom accident or a mistaken partiality
has placed for a season in the South and West? And thus, if the usefulness of
the Institution is really advancf!d, at the present time, by the selection of the
most capable and best informed brethren to preside over and cond11ct its Lodges,
without reference to the stations they may previously have occupied, is not the
spirit and 1intent of the ancient charge effectually maintained, although it be
apparently violated in the letter ? It seems to us that it is ; and in any event,
we do not a·t all jloubt that it is far better for the honor, the utility, the respectability, the perpetuity of Masonry, that an educated, zealous, and intelligen1;
brother of a single month's standing in the Order, should be elevated to the
Mastership, rather than an ignorant, careless, or stupid individual, who may have
been a Mnson for twenty years, and whose only qualification is that by some
untoward misfortune to the Craft be bus been once a Waiden. All this, too, is
upon the supposed proposition that the "Old Charges" absolutely required that
a Master should' first have served as Warden. But there is room for doubt
whether or not that might have been intended to be merely suggestive that
one who bad thus served would probably be the fittest for the higher office. The
fourth of the" Old Charges,"- the one which contains this so-called regulation
-commenceR as follows: "All preferment among Masons is grounded upon
real worth and personal merit 011ly ; • • • • • 'I'herifore 110 Master or Warden
is chosen by seniority, but for his mtrit." Now this would seem to say that a Warden
is not necessarily to be selected from among the eldest of the brethren, but from
rtmong the best of them; and that a Master also is not impemtively to be taken
from among those who have occupied the office next in rank, but from those best
qualified to discharge the duties of the position. This, to be sure, is at variance
with the apparent positiveness of the words which soon after follow - " No
brother can be a Warden until be has pas.~ed the part of a Fellow-Craft, or a
Master until he bas acted as a Warden " ; bnt if the two passages 'cannot be
reconciled to mean that a Warden should be elected Master in preference to any
other brother, equally capable -not for bis " seniority, but for bis merit " -then
we prefer to consult the real good of the Order by acting only under the sensible proposition laid down in the commencement of the charge. A word or two

more in reg1trd to that which we have called an erroneous definition by our

the plain language of those ancient records, that Fellow-Crafts were the very
Masons from among whom Wardens were chosen, and it strikes us that Bro. DossoN
has interpolated a very original definition to the words "has passed the part of
a Fellow-Craft," when he announces them to mean "has become a Master Mason." If any proof were needed that those words mean simply that a Warden
should hiwe passed to the degree of Fellow-Craft, it is foood in the second line
below them in the same "Old Charge," where it is written that a brother cannot
be Grand Master "unless he has been a Fellow-Orajt before his election," &c. Thus,
if no higher degree was necessary to enable him to reach that exalted office, it
is scarcely probable that it was required to quality him for the comparatively.
humble position of Warden of a Lodge. But this is not left even to any supposition of probability. In the succeeding "Charge," the fifth, it is written that
"when a Fellow-Oraftsman is chos~n Warden of the work uuder the Master, he
Rhall be true both to Master and Fellows, &c.," thus showing that Fellow-Crafts
alone, (and not Master Masons, as Bro. Dos1.<0N has most inventively suggested},
were at that time selected for that office. To close the argument, it is only necessary to say that in the days when the "Old Charges" were set forth, we do
not hear of the degree of " Master Mason." Entered Apprentices were made
in the several private Lodges, and they were Mas(}tls. The degree of FellowCraft was conferred in the Grand Lodge, (when it was established), and from
among those the Wardens and Jfasters were seleeted; and the last,-mean!ng
the Masters of Lodges, - were chosen from among those who had served in the
office next in rank, for the good reaeon that in those days they were beyond
doubt the most likely to be the best qualified to perform the duties of the office.

Bro. MUNRO also requests the Grand Lodge to decide" whether, after a candidate
has been elected, he can be rejected, and objections raised by a brother who was
not present when the ballot was passed," and also whether " it is proper and
legal, after a ballot has been passed at one regular meeting, at the next reirular
meeting to move a reconsideration of the vote, and pass the ballot again.ff So
far as the first question concerns a candidate for the initiatory degree we understand the received opinion to be that any member may veto his initlation as
peremptorily as he might have done at the ballot; but for the subsequent degrees, different opinions are held by Masonic writers-some asserting the same
imperative right as in the first, and others, more correctly as we think declaring that, as the applicant is already a Mason, he has certain rights which are
not thus summarily to be 1lisposed of, and that in such cases- some examination
should be bad in regard to the rea8ons of the objection. As to the second question, it needs no argument to show the impropriet:y of the proposition, as were
it admitted, a Lodge might go on balloting for, rejecting, and reconsidering the
ballot for the same candidate at every regular meeting for a whole generation.
The Report on Foreign Correspondence is presented, as during the two or
three years preceding, by the Grand Secretary, Bro. JAMES FENTON. It is rather
short, giving little more than the names of the various Grand Lodges with a
few quotations from some of their proceedings. The only opinion f~om the
Committee which appears to have been offered in the report, is a recommendation that the Grand Lodge of Kansas be not acknowledged, upon the ground "that
the true Masonic law does not recognise the right of any but sovereign and independent States to form a Grand Lodge." We would be obliged to our learned
brother of Michigan if' he would inform us where that "true Masonic law" is to
be found, or where there is any Masonic law at all upon the subject, other than
the custom which has grown up in the United States with the circumstances
which have created so many new Grand Lodges in the Territories as well as in
the States. Perhaps Bro. FENTON would at the same time give us his opinion in
regard to the consistency of the Grand Lodge of Michigan, which adopts his report, with this recommendation, and in the same publication which presents that
action, enumerates among the Grand Lodges in correspondence with itself those
of the District of Columbia, and the Territories of Minnesota and Oregon'?
Amendments to the Constitution were adopted, requiring a candidate to have
resided six months within the jurisdiction of the Lodge to which his application
was made, to render him eligible i and authorizing the subordinate Lodges to
publish the names of any expelled members, with the reasons for the expulsion
upon the concurrence of two thirds of the members present at the time of' such
action. An amendment which bad been proposed, making all Past Masters full
members of the Grand Lodge, was most properly rejected.
We remark a case where a member of' a Lodge in one section of the State
was trled by another distant Lodge within whose jurisdiction he resided and
was expelled for unmasonic conduct. An appeal was presented upon the gr~und
that none but the Lod~e of which the accused was a member had the right to
try hlm, but the committee to whom the matter was referred reported, corre~tly
as we think, that every Mason was subject to discipline by the Lodge witbi~
whose jurisdiction he had taken up bis residence, and the Grand Lodge, as correctly, adopted the report. The Grand Treasurer's exhibit shows that the receipts for the year were $1923-that the expenditures for the same period were
$1970- and that there remained in the Treasury a balance of $569. Ninety- .

passing ordinances upon subjects which were the laws of Masonry and of morality long before Grand Lodges were ever heard of. The grave enactments of
Masonic legislatures that a violation of the moral law is really immoral, is not
only ridiculou~, but worse, as it may well leave the inference upon the minds
of the uninitiated that the remarkable fact is a new discovery by our Conscript
Fathers, and that the c!mduct of Masons requires especial guardianship in such
respects. We have heretofore expressed our opinions at length upon this matter,
. and are pleased with the conclusion of Bro. WH1TCOMB, "that temperance is
taught by our ritual and should be strictly observed, but we very much doubt
the proprietT or •usefulness of Gmnd Lodges passing so many resolutions upon
the subject.' The question relative to the recognition of' the Grand Lodge of
Canada is briefly noticed, and after enumerating the Grand Lodges which had
taken action upon that subject, so far as heard from, it is declared that there is
no occasion for the Grand Lodge of Missouri " to take any further steps at present." This appears to have been the opinion of the Grand Lodge, as we do not
see that the subject was elsewhere mentioned during its Communication. The
subjects of uniformity of work, and of the proper boundaries of Masonic jurisdictions, are treated in the same manner as the others, but as neither of these things
have much interest for us here, we not now being troubled on the one score or
the other, we simply express the opinion that in regard to the last, the only certain course to avoid difficulty and annoyance is a rigid adherence to the State
or Territorial lines which mark the political boundaries within which the Grarid
Lodge is situated. The report concludes with some remarks upon the . general
J!.lanner of constituting, and the onerous labors of, a Committee on Foreign
Correspondence, which are so sensible that no false modesty shall prev11nt our
copying them in full.
" We think the~present system defective. A committee is appointed, but one person,
the chairman, does all the work, and it is really his report. Frequ11ntly a very incoll)i>etent- or, as m our case, an ioexperiencP.d-brother is selected as the chairmell, and
the report is anvthing else than a review of the workings of the Craft. Some hobbyhorse 1s mounted.-some one idea is got after and chased to the end of the reportwith little benefit to the wciter, and much less to the reader. Sometimes it is of the
snapping-turtle order, like that of our brother HACKJrn, of Indiana, or is as misanthropic
88 the one by our Delaware brother, who must have been very bilious when he wrote it.
The pl11n we suggest is the one adopted by South Carolina, California, lllinois, Michigan,
New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oregon and Vermont, to make the Grand Secretary
chairman of the committee; or, what would be better, because more simple, either to
Jet him make a report on Foreigu Correspondence, or, if the duties would be too onerous,
have a Corresponding Grand Secretary for that especial purpose. But, whether the
Grand Secretary makes the report, or it be made by the chauman of a committee, as at
present, let th€m be paid, as they are in Maine, Tennessee, Connecticut, (New York) Rnd
some other State•. We speak from experience when we say that oo one can afford to
faithfully do his duty, analyze the proceedings of the several Grand Lodges, and make
such a report as the brethren ought to have, without remuneration; and we speak freely,
because under no circumstances will we again attempt to discharge the duty.''

Another has been added to the Registry of American Grand Lodges-the
thirty-sixth of the list-and cordially as we last year welcomed the Supreme
Masonic organization of her political twin-sister, Kansas, do we now extend our
greetings to the Grand Lodge of Nebraska.
On the twenty-third day of September, 1857, the Masters and Wardens of the
three Lodges then existing in Nebraska, viz. :-Nebraska Lodge, No. 184, chartered by Illinoi&-Giddings Lodge, No. 156, chartered by :Missouri-and Capital
Lodge, No. 101., chartered by Iowa, assembled at Omalia City; and iu all proper
form, so far as appears from the record now before us, formed and opened a Grand
Lodge for that Territory, and elected and inetallP.d its officers. A Constitution
By-Laws and Il.ules of Order-for the Grand Lodge, and Rules and Regulation~
for the government of its subordinates, were adopted. In the first we are pleased
to see that our Nebraska brethren have profited in one respect by the unlucky
experience of some of their elders. and have left out Past Masters from the membership of the Grand Lodge,/ thus probably sparing tbemsel.ves much future
trouble. On the other hand, we regret the announcement in the organic law
that it is the prerogative of the Grand Master "to make Masons at sight " and
cannot but consider it as unnecessary or unwise, or both. If Grand M.ast~rs, by
virtue of their office, really possess such a "prerogative," as Is claimed by some
then it was most unnecessary to enact that which was already a foregone conclu~
sion. If they do not, was it not unwise to plnce such needless power in bis
bands, and thus, from the highest source, eet the.example of removing the careful
guards around the doors of' initiation which it is, or ought to be the constant
duty of the F'raternity to maintain? What need is there in these days, when in
every State and Territory a Lodge Is to be found within easy reach of all, that
Masons ~hould be made at sight ? If the Grand Master for the time be really a
good Mason, it is not probable that be will ever use the power thus acknowledged, as lie will properly prefer that candidates should pass through the
ordeal oi inquiry among their neighbors and acquaintances, as prescribed by our
general usages. If' he be not, which may sometimes happen, it is not difficult to
see bow dangerous and unfortunate for our Order, the uncontrolled exercise of
such authority may become. The provision is, in our opinion, both unwise and
unnecessary, and we can only hope that naught may occur in Nebraska to make
it more than a dead letter in the law.
•

member. But it is further ''made the imperative duty of the Master to cause
the Secretary to enter 'suspended' every member who shall be in arrears and
fo~thwith to notify him of the same; and if, within a reasonable time there~fter
as the Lodge may determine, the member so suspended does not dirnbar"'e hi~
dues, he shall be expelled." In the Rules of Order it is declared that the Grand
Master "shall be the judge of order and debate. When his decision is fairly

The twentieth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Texas w*!

.
The Address of the Grand Master is of more than ordinary length, and of
vei;y much more th~n ~rdinary ability. It is refreshing to see occasionally a well
written paper of this krnd, and we wish that we could more frequently find tliat
pleas?re in. reading Marnnic mesmges which we have experienced in the perusal
of this. The decease of two distinguished Past Grand Masters of that juriEdietion, Bros. JAMES WEBB and BRANCH T. ARCHER, is appropriately announced, and
an eloquent tribute ia given to their memory. A prohibition of itinerant lecturing is recommended, and, as will hereafter be seen, the Grand Lodge adopted a
resolution to carry the suggestion into eft€ct. Several pages are devoted to the
.details of his official action in regard to the delinquencies, or alleged delinquen•
ci~s, ?f sundry Lodges; and .we mention this only for the purpose of rnying that
this ts one of the very few instances we have seen where such merely domestiQ
matters are presented in a manner so attractive as to make them interesting t•
the foreign reader. One of these cases, however, was of more than ordinary im-portance,-affecting in its decision, not alone the juriEdiction of Texas, but the
whole body of the Fraternity. It arose from the act of a Lodge in conferring
tfle three degrees. of MaEOnry upon a man who avowed that he "did not believe
the Bible to be the revealed will of God," nor "that God had ever made any
revelation of his will to man"; and it elicited a long and interesting argumen~
from tile Gi;and Master upon the question whether a candidate should, or Ehould
not be reqmred to express a belief that the Bible is of Divine origin. In it he
shows conclusively that in all Ohriatian lands the Scripture~ have ever held
the most prominent consideration in a Lodge, and that (in such countries) a Mason's belief in its contents (or some portion of them) is necessarily to be inferred
But he adds :-'"It rRn not, I think, he sucre••fully claimed that a Mason of the three symbolic de·
grces must necessarily admit the Divine authority of the New Teslament1 or the truth of

301

the !'ume~ous religious doctrines which are deduced from it by as many religious sects.
l thmk this clear, because I do not believe that there is any portion of the liistory, leelures, ceremonies, teachings, or usages of Ancient Craft Masonry, which can not be
fully explained, understood, and pracl!ced without reference to the New Testament.''
Now this, so far as it relates to our own country, coincides with our own opini?n. Our pr~ncipal objection. to the Ohio doctrine is, that it ·requires the expreEs1on of a behef mall the Scriptures, both Old and New, and thus absolutely limits Freemasonry to the professors of the Christian faith ; but our general objection
to the whole proposition is that it introduces a test which for ages has not been
considered necessary, and which, by connecting Masonry with particular religions, will result in the destruction of that universality which is now, and has ever
been its most important and useful characteristic. The Grand Master expresses
the opinion that Lodges have multiplied with too great rapidity in Texas, and
presents a picture of some of them which fully justifies the declaration. H,e declares his conviction that the system of District Deputy Grand Masters is a
most useful one ; presents some very sensible suggestions in regard to that great
desideratum-uniformity of work ; and announces the issue of ten Dispensations
to form new Lodges. To these are to be added five more issued"by the Deputy
Grand Master.
The Report on Foreign Correspondence is presented by Bro. WM. STEDMAN,
the Grand Master elect at this Communication. It needed not the apologetic in,
troduction with which it commences, for, (and we say it at the risk of being again
charged by our brethren in Texas with the expression of opinions ex cathedra)
there are few better ones to be met. He, too, writes at considerable length in
approval of the Ohio test, but as he says he speaks only of Ohriatian Masonry,
leaving the inference,-in fact absolutely arguing-that there is no other real Masonry, we have naught to offer in reply. We do know one essentially Christian Order
of Masonry, but to that Masonry of. the symbolic degrees which these reports alone
refer to, we acknowledge no particular religious or sectarian prefix. It is possible
that by-and-by we may hear of Episcopalian, Methodist, and Baptist Masonry, and
that, at a still later period, further discriminating distinctions may be known
under the appropriate heads of High and Low Church Masonry,-Methodist Masonry, North and South,-and Baptist Masonry of both the Hard and Soft shell
varieties. It is to be hoped that it may not be so, but the late remarkable discovery. that Masonry, without knowing it, has been so irreligious during many
centuries, may engender further new and yet more singular ones, until, in the
fulness of time, the apparently absurd possibilities which we have suggested shall
be brought to light. At the conclusion of his argument upon this subject, Bro.
STEDMAN proposed the following resolution :" That the Grand Lodge of Texas declares that a distinct avowal of a belief in the
Divine authenticity of the Holy Scriptures is an indispensable prA·requisjte to Masonic admission in all Clmstian countries; and that it shall not be lawful, within her jurisdiction,
lo initiate, pas11, or raise a person who does not entertain that belief."
This was referred to the committee upon the Grand Officers' Reports, who
reported in its stead another resolution, which was adopted by the Grand Lodge,
as follows!"Resolved, That the Grand Lodge of 'l'exas declares that a belief in the Divine authenticity of the Holy Scriptures is an indiepensable pre-requisite to Masonic admission;
and the Grand Lodge does not mean lo exclude the Israelite, whom it does not regard as
disqualified for the mysteries of Freemasonry."
Now the intent of this resolution is obvious. The Grand Lodge had appa-'
rently adopted the conclusion of the Grand Master, that a belief in. the Divine
origin of tire Old Testament alone was necessary, and it was doubtless intended
to enact that proposition. With no desire to look unnecessarily for faults in the
legislation of our esteemed sister of Texas, and with every sentiment of respect
and courtesy, we ask if it so reads. The first sentence of the resolution imperatively declares that a belief in the Divine authority of both the Testaments is requisite-for the term "the Holy Scriptures" includes the two ; while the concluding portion proceeds with a copulative conjunction to assert that such a

belief in both is not in all cases to be required ! There appears to be a sliding
scale of qualification. A Christian must subscribe to both the Testaments-a. Jew
to only one. By the same tariff of creeds, we see no reason why a Turk should
be required to pretend a belief in either. All believe in God, and we see no reason
to alter our opinion that all, thus believing, who, in the language of the first Old
Charge, are "good men and true, or men of honor and honesty, by whatever denominations or persuasions they may be distinguished," are eligible candidates for
the mysteries of Masonry ; for it is by this means, in the words of the rnme
charge, that "Masonry becomes the centre of union, and the means of conciliating true friendship among persons that must else have remained at a perpetual
distance."
The language of the Texan committee in regard to the Grand Lbdge of California is flattering in the extreme. "The proceedings before us," say the committee, "contain abundant evidence that no Grand Lodge in the world is graced
with a higher order of talent, a more thorough familiarity with Masonic law and
philosophy, and a juster appreciation of MaEOnic behest and obligation, than that
which distinguishes our sister jurisdiction of California"; and our own humble
but zealous labors are spoken of in terms too complimentary to be repeated here.
Yet while our natural modesty forbids us to mention the good things said of us,
a proper humility requires that we should note and profit by such censure as it
may appear to our brethren abroad that we have deserved. In the midst of many
k~nd expressions it is remarked by Bro. STEDMAN, that " it is to be regretted that
Bro. ABELL, by sometimes assuming an ex cathedra tone, and at others, by the use
of EOme cant phrase, or inelegant expression, should break the force and weaken
the influence of one of the most learned, profound, and logical MaEOnic papers
that it has been our good fortune to meet with." As to the first charge! it may
be true, and if it is, we regret it. When, in 1855, we commenced the preparation
of the reports on Foreign Correspondence to the Grand Lodge of California, we
had very little personal experience in Masonic matters, und naught to guide us
but an attentive reading of one of the best collections of Masonic works in the
United States, and such common sense and powers of reasoning as nature und
education had afforded us. With great distrust, therefore, in our own conelusione,
we endeavored to present such opinions as, from these sources, we bud formed, in
the suggestive and deferential manner which properly befitted our inexperience
and unknown name. This course we have ever intended to continue, not only
because it best became our comparatively limited and imperfect knowledge of the
subjects upon which we write, but because we are well aware that a good argument or correct opinion may frequently be diminished in its force or destroyed in
its effect, when presented in a manner offensively arrogant or positive. We had
hoped not to fall into this too common error, but us it seems we have, we cun only
express our sorrow, and in all sincerity, promise Bro. STEDMAN that we will endeavor to profit by the fraternal reproof. To the second charge, preferred b1, our
esteemed brother of Texas, we are compelled to put in the plea of "guilty, ' but
with extenuating circumstances. In fact, we were on the point of increasing our
culpability by thoughtlessly declaring that we "acknowledge the corn"; but, as
will be seen, we have checked ourselves in the utterance. There is no defence
for the use of inelegant language in writing by those whose acquirements should
prompt the use of better, nor do we mean to attempt any. llut it does sometimes
happen, when, doffing for the moment the severer panoply of argument and words
of wisdom, and indulging briefly in a playful vein, that a current phrase, though
perhaps unpolished and altogether homely, is more ef!ective in the conveyance of
an idea than a whole paragraph of Johnson's most proper and pompous pollysyllables. On such occasions we have prollably Himetimes used such language ;
but it may well be that the practice would have been "more honored in the
breach than the observance." We take the suggestion in the ~ame kind spirit which
has evidently induced it, and if the hurry of scribbling the couple of hundred
pages of manuscript required for one of these reports will permit, it shall be
borne in memory hereafter.

accordance with this order the Warrants of thirty-eight Lodges were surrendered, being all apparently there represented; and then, without a charter in.existence, it was resolved that the "Ancient Grand Lodge of Canada " be formed,
and that S111. ALLAN N. McNAB be its first Grand Master. We have not time
now to express our opinions in regard to the manner of the organization. Fortyseven Lodgea appear to adhere to it, and the late Pcovincial Grand Secretary,
the v.., W:. FRANCIS R1CBARDSON, was appointed to fulfil the same duties in the
new body.
CONCLUSION.
The committee had cherished the hope of being enabled at this Communication to present, in exteMo, the whole subject of the Canadian difficulties, with such
opinions as they have formed in regard to it, and the reasons from which they are
deduced. But domestic affiictio[IS have deprived them of the time necessary for
ihe creditable accomplishment of that purpose, and the hour is now at hnnd
when this report must be concluded. This much, however, they briefly 1ay.
The developments of the past year ha-Ve placed the organizations in C&!iada
in a position, as regards each other, differing greatly from that they occupied at
the da.te of our last review. Then there was a ProTlncial Grand Body of undoubted legality in existence, which still numbered among the subordinatPA
who adhered to more than half of those existing in the Upper Province ; and,
though all our warmest sympathies were aroused at tho eloquent and truthful
manner in which the new Grand Lodge had set forth the grievances which impelled the declaration of its independence. we did not think it right to desert
those who, notwithstanding the many evils of which they also loudly complah;1ed,
remained thus sturdily faithful to the Masonic precept of obedience. Now the
RCenes are shifted and the characters are changed. The Provincial Grand Lodge,
after receiving concessions from the Grand ·Master of England which included
all the privileges it prayed for two years before, and which, had they been granted thenJ would doubtless have prevented the secession of those who formed · tho
Grand Lodge of Canada, increased its demands to the extent of an absolute
recognition of its independent existence; and, upon its being rendered probable
that such an acknowledgment would not be obtained, first negotiated with the
body it had previously outlawed, and then, with less provocation than the other,
followed in its footsteps. Thus we have a choice of two organ!:Gatlons - the
Grand Lodge of Canada, and the Ancient Grand Lodge of Canada - both
formed by a violent separation from the parent body to which their constituent~
principally owed allegiance, and, In that respect, both standing upon a position
of equality before us. We must recognize one or the other, or ignore the existence of Masonry in Canada, except so far as the limited jurisdiction of tho
Provincial Grand LodJ1,'es of Montreal and William Henry, and Quebec, and
Three Rivers are concerned. The last altenatlve we have no thought of adopting, and as between the two Grand Lodges, we have no hesitation In giving
preference to the first. Our opinions in regrud to the propriety of its formation
had undergone some change before learning the action of the late Provinc!nl
Grand Lodge, and now we have no room for doubt as to our choice of action.
We recommend the recognition of that Grand Lodie of Canada of which the
M.'. W:. WM. MERCER WILSON is Grand Master, and the R:. W:. THos. BIRD HAR•
ms is Grand Secretary.
It is a subject of regret, not only that we have been compelled thus hurriedly
to speak of a matter of such importance ; but that our foreign communications
must remain unnoticed, further th&n the simple acknowledgment of their receipt
contained in the commencement of this paper. Indeed, the writer has much to
nsk indulgence for throughout the whole of the report. It·has been written at
vnrious intervals, during a period of grievous sadness and anxiety, while watching by the sick-bed of one most near and dear ; and it is scarcely possible that
justice has been done to any of the subjects where argument or reasoning has
been attempted. It Is believed, however, to be a faithful summary of the proceedings of those Grand bodies which it professes to review, and as such It is
presented to the Grand Lodge of Califorma.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
ALEX. G. ABELL, Chairman.

In less than three years this Grand Lodge has cancelled disagreeable pecuniary obligatlons, made liberal appropriations of its revenue, and yet acquired to itself the complacent assumnce of having a surplus

Under such circumstances your committee fe el like terminati ng their report
iu a rhapsody of congratulation; but a sense of harsh and disagreeable d\,lty will
not permit the indulgence. There are still incursive evils leaving their unnecessary traces upon the financial economy of onr Grand Lodge. And, as financial
committees are generally composed of men who arc commonly esteemed in proportion as they succeed in r epresenting the spirit of censorial grumblers, we
must crowd the poetry of our feelings into the chilling retreats of suspicion and
censure.
The Grand Lodge spends too much money, and is too little governed by the
limited appropriations which are annually adopted for its guide. Last year the

Now your committee would ask what have been the expenditures, exclusive
of $2000 invested 1 The answer is $7523 56 ; an excess of $1523 56 over the
fixed appropriations for the year. Whose fault is this? Is it to be charged to
the Grand Master, or Grand Secretary, or Grand Treasurer ? Not at all. It is
to be charged to the Grand Lodge itself in its constituent character-to a lack
of reference to the limits which have been unanimously erected, when propositions for appropriations are presented for tlle consideration of' the Grand Lodge.
In those appeals, which in all bodies of this kind are multiplied in proportion as
they are liberally responded to, we forget our resolutions of economy, and
launch out into an extravagance equal to t.he generous and munificent donations
of a man revelling in the dreams of a Sir John Barleycorn. Instead of an excess
of $1523,56, it is a wonder that the sum is not $2523,56. Now what shall we
do? Shall we cut down the Grand Secretary's salary, which is the largest special appropriation? . Your committee answer most emphatically, NO. We want

1b the M." W. •. Grand Lodge of California :Your Committee, to whom was referred a circ11lar from a Committee of the
M:. W.". Grand Lodge of Maine, and an accompanying resolution of that Grand
Body, urging the formation of a General Grand Lodge, "at the time and place
of meeting of the General Grand Chapter and General Grand Encampmeµt, in
September, 1859," beg leave .respectfully to report, that after due consideration
of the matter, they have arrived at the conclusion that the formation of such a
body is at this time impracticable, and that therefore its further consideration by
this Grand Lodge is inexpedient. The failures which have heretofore attended
every effort directed in that behalf, and the non-concurrence of a large majority
of the Grand Lodges of the United States in the Articles of Confederation propo~ed in the conve11tions heretofore assembled, in the opinion of your committee
plainly Indicate that the direction of the general sentiment of the Craft is adverse to the formation of such a body, and ebadow forth what is likely to be the
result of any other convention which might be assembled at the time proposed
for a similar purpose. As the past will show that we cannot reasonably expect
o.n active representatfon in a Masonic Convention held at a great distance from
us, without sending delegates for the.t especial ~urpose, whose expenses would
necessarily be heavy, and must of course be paid, we think it inexpedient and
unadvisable to subject the Grand Lodge to such expense, where there is no probability of an accruing benefit.
Could your Committee be assured that a General Grand Lodge of the United
States could be formed, clothed with limited and strictly defined powers, such
a~, while giving it efficiency as a dernier re:iort for the final settlement of such
Masonic difficulties as might with propriety be brought forward for its action,
as the Supreme Head of Symbolic Masonry for the regulation of its work and
lecture~, and the establishment of uniformity throughout the United States
would at the same time deprive it of all power for evif, by an abuse of author!~
ty or a centralization of power, they would cheerfully advocate the assembling
of another Convention for that purpose. But, believing as they do, that "a
consummation so devoutly to be wished" is at this time wholly lmpra.cticable
and also for other reasons aBsigned, they would respectfully recommend that n~
further action be at prescn t bad in reference thereto.
All of which is respectfully submitted.

Bro. WM. H. HOWARD, from the Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence, presented the following report : 'lb the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of Oalifrmiia :-

Your Committee, to whom was referred certain portions of the Grand Master's
Address, (some of which they have already reported upon), having duly considered the remaining references, beg leave to report as follows:They approve of the refusal of the Grand Master to grant dispensations ""for
the conferring the degrees in less time than that provided by the Constitution," but
would not be understood as doubting bis prerogative to do so, if, in his judgment, be had deemed it expedient and proper ; and are of opinion that no emergency has arisen during bis term of service which would have rendered such
t\ction on his part advisable.
They a1;>prove, also, of his refusal to grant dispensations " for a re-ballot for
persons rejected within the time prescribed by the Constitution," but assert
his prerogative to have done so had he seen proper. One of your committee, as
the Grand Lodge is aware, has been placed in a position to render a just appre·
ciation of the Grand Master's action in reference to this, as well as other matters,
at least supposable. Having grantea several diBpensations to ballot for rejected
applicants, at the earnest solicitation of divers LodgeB, and upon what seemed
to be good and sufficient grounds, he was pained to learn, in due course of time,
that in more than one instance the privilege thus conferred bad been abused,
and advantage taken of the absence of an objecting brother, or other improper
appliances used to foist upon the Fraternity an unacceptable and perhaps an
unworthy applicant, He took occasion, at an early day, to 'confer with the
present M:. W.-. Grand Master In relation thereto, and was gratified to learn
from him that they coincided in opinion as to the Inexpediency of granting
dispensations for such purposes.
As regards "a thorough revision of the standing resolutions," and "a repeal
of tbe resolution permitting the subordinate Lodges to ballot for the three
degrees at the same time," your committee would remark ibat they seem to be
referred to by the Grand Master, in connexion with the consideration and final
action in reference to the new Constitution, which it was supposed would take
place during the present Communication; and, as that matter has been laid over
until the next Annual Communication, your committee would recommend that a
similar disposition be made of these also, by referring them to a special committee to revise, condense and report them at that time.
All of which is respedfully submitted.
W. H. HOWARD,
)
J, R. CRANDALr,,
A. HoLLUB,
Cbmmittee.

1

day of February, 1858, he was summoned by Waahington Lodge to show cause
why ht; should not be stricken from its roll for non-payment of dues. It then
appearmg that he was holding membership iu Concord Lodge, claim was made on
said Lodge by direction of the Worshipful Master of Washington Lodge, for this
am~unt- the claim b_ein~ based upon the provisions of the 9th section of
Article X. of the Coostitutwn, and the 70th Stnndlng Resolution of the Grand
Lodge.
·
Your committee are of the opinion that the case in question does not fall
within ihe provisions of the Constitution and Standing Resolution above referred
to, believing that they are to be construed ns applying exclusively to the recep~ion into members~ip by affiliation ; and that Concord Lodge therefore is not
Indebted to Washington Lodge for the amount of the dues of the delinquent
brother, but that such dues remain a personal claim against the brother, who has
never been received into legal membership in Concord Lodge.
Holding, therefore, that the fact of a brother naming himself in a petition,
or being named in a Dispensation for 11. new Lodge, would not render such
Lodge liable for his indebtedness to his former Lodge, and anxious to prevent
the recurrence of questions of this nature, yonr committee recommend the adop·
tion of the following resolution : Resolved, That hereafter all petitioners for a Dispensation, who are members
of .Lodges within this jurisdiction, be required to state In their petition the
names and numbers of the respective Lodges to which they Inst belonged, and
to accompany the same with certificates from tho Secretaries thereof that they
arc free from all indebtedness to the same.

which is ~o eminently characteristic of our Order.
The Grand Orient of France, in proposin1r this system of Representatives, has

propose and carry into effect a plan for the assembling of 11 Universal Masonic
Congress, the first whereof convened in Paris, in 1855, and' was attended by a
large body of representatives from different parts of the world. We deem the
interest displayed by the Grand Orient of France on all Masonic subjects, highly
to be commended, and as affording a gratifying proof of the flourishing condition
or the Order in that Empire. The action of the Grand Master of Masons in
this State, in promptly replying to the suggestion of the Grand Master of France,
meets with our fullest approbation ; and we trust that the system now so haprily
initiated, may prove a mutual source of pleasure and fraternal aid to both Grand

Bro. J . .A. RAYMOND, from the Committee .on Education, presented the following report : 1b the }If,., w. .. Grand Lodge of Oalifornia:Your Committee on Education beg leo.ve to report that they have had that
subject under consideration, and present the following conclusions:In the present Rtate of the funds of the Grand Lodge, the establishment of a
seminary of learning or a Masonic college, even if desiro.ble, seems quite impracticable; and it is not at a.II clear to your committee that a necessity ex.ists for
any course of education, or any school or system of schools, separate from those
already in existence. They believe that the very wise and ample provisions or
our State government for the free education of all classes of children, whether
under the special care of this Fraternity or not, are quite sufficient to meet all
our wants ; and while this is the case, any attempt on our part to compete with
such system, or any course which looks like a desire on the part of Ma~oory to
be exclusive in its educational plans, will not be likely to commend our Order
to the favor of the public, nor give the subjects of our charge any desirable
distinction. Your commltt.ee are of opinion that the ordinary Masonic attention
to the education· of each individual case, as it may arise1 in the common schools
provided for the people, without attempting the erection of a new school, or
identifying ourselves with any tio.rticular one now in existence, will accompli@h
for the present the full measure of our duty, while it may save us from much
unmerited censure and unnecessary trouble.
While your committee arc fully convinced of the adaptation of the above
principles to the present circumstances, we would by no mcan8 intimate that the
time mo.y not come when the donation of land so generously tendered by a
brother for the erection of a university under the charge of the Fraternity, may
be rendered available and be made to accompllsh the full measure of good anticipated by the donor.
All of which is respectfully submitt~d.
Jom; A. ToTT,
J, A. RAYMOND, } Ocnnmittee.
DARWIN CHASE,

1b the ltf. •• W.·. Grand Lodge of Cal,ifwnia :Your Committee, to whom was referred the petition of D. N. ALLAN, asking

CHARLES RAISH,
To the M.-. W.·. Grand Lodge of Otllifornia:Your Committee, to whom was referred the appeal of CHARLES B. UBL,
in the matter of his suspension by We&ern Star Lodge, No. 2, have had the same
under consideration. The error complained of is that hearsay evidence was
received. The evidence upon which the verdict was rendered not having been
sent up with the papers, we have no means of ascertaining whether the alleged
error is true, or whether there was sufficient testimony independent of any hearsay evidence, to sustain the verdict. The accused, in taking the appeal, did all
that he was required to do. It wus the duty of the Lodge to have sent up the
evid~nce. That having been neglected, the accused should not be made to suffer
or be deprived of his rights by having his sentence confirmed without a review
of the proceedings. As that cannot be had at this session of the Grand Lodge,
we deem it better to reverse the sentence and send the case back for a new trial.
We therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution:Resolved, That the suspension of CHARLES B. UHL, be and the same iR hereby
reversed and set aside, and that the case be remanded for a new trial.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
JAMES L. Eimr.1sH, }
L. BATES,

E. W. ROBERTS,

the proceedings of the Grand Lodge, as well as all documents issued under its
authority, and directed to its subordinates, should be read in open Lodge. They
do recommend, however, that said rcsolntion be amended so as to read as

Master, and within the period of three months from the time of then· reception,

1b the JI.:. W. ·.Grand Lodge of California :Your Committee, to whom was referred a resolution providing for the amendiug of Standing Resolution No. 34, so as" to include and discourage the use of
Masonic emblellljl on business cards and jewelry," having given the subject tlue
consideration, beg leave to report that they would not recommend any further
legislation in reference to that subject ; the resolution proposed to be a.mended
being in their opinion. sufficiently expressive of the unqualified disapprove.I by
this Grand Lodge of such exhibitions. Your committee are moreover of opinion
that the day is not far distant when the evil complained of will, in all probability correct itself as the general sentiment of the Craft is becoming more and
mo're adverse to ~uch displays, and as it is believed thnt they even now Injure
the exhibitor far more than they benefit him.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
w. H.. HowARD, Uhairman.

Bro. WM. H. HOWARD, from the same committee, also presented
the following report : Jb the M:. W." GrtJnd Lodge of CaUf'ornia:Your Committee, to whom was referred a resolution suggesting the repeal
of Standing Resolution No. 22, having given the matter due consideration, beg
leave to report that they do not see any impropriety in a Mason belonging to
a subordinate Lodge in o.nother jurisdiction as well as in this, " provided he be
in good standing In his original Lodge, and pays his dues regularly in both."
There is no general law of the Craft which would render such membership im·
proper, and it must, th~refore , be viewed in the light of its expediency a.lone ;
and, as your committee are unable to point to an instance where difficulties have
arisen in connexion with such membership, which were not attributable to other
ca.uses, they would recommend that Standing Resolution, No. 22, be left in its
present shape.
•
All of which is respectfully submitted.
W. H. HowARD, Chairman.

ARTICLE III.
MEETI!<US OF THE GRJ.ND LOllUE.

SECTION 1. The Annual Communications of the Grand Lodge ehall be held in
the City of Sacramento, on the second Tuesday of May, in each year.
SEc. 2. The Grand Master, (or in-his absence from the State, or inability to
attend, the Deputy Grand Master,) upon the application of the presiding officers
of any three Lodges under this juriediction, shall call special meetings of' the
Grand Lodge.
ARTICLE IV.
l!JU:CTION OF GR.I.ND OFFI<;Eil.S.

SECTION I. The Most Worshipful Grand Master, Right Worshipful Deputy
Grand Master, Rlirht Worshipful Senior and Junior Grand Wardens, Right
Worshipful Grand Treasurer, and Right Worshipful Grand Secretary, ehall be
elected at each Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, on the fourth day
of' its sitting, and shall hold their respective offices until their successors are
duly elected and installed. A majority of all the votes cast at an election for
Grand Officers, shall be necessary for a choice. All other Grand Officers shull
be appointed in such manner ns the Grand Lodge may direct.
I
S.11:c. 2. No brother shall be ellgible to au elective office unless he is a Present
or Past Master, nor entitled to membership in the Grand Lodge, unless a member of a subordinate Lodge under this jurisdiction.
ARTICLE V.
VOTING.
SECTION I. Each of' the Grand Officers for the time being, and every elective Past Grand Officer present at a meeting of the Grand Lodge, shall be entitled to one vote. Each Lodge shall be entitled to three votes by its proper
officers, or in their absence, their proper representatives ; and the Past Masters,
by service, of each Lodge, collectively, to one vote. No member, of his own
right, shall be entitled to more than one vote.
SEc. 2. In all questions except thoBe decided by ballot, in the event of a tie,
the presiding officer shall have the casting vote:
8Ec. 3. No Lodge under this jurisdiction and within this State, shall be repre~en ted by a proxy who is not u member of the Lodge.
ARTICLE VI.
STANDING COMMITTEES.

SECTION I. At each meeting of the Grand Lodge, the Grand Master or presiding officer shall appoint the following committees, each to consist of not less
tha~ three nor more thnn five members, viz.:A Committee on Credentials.
A Committee on Grievances.
A Committee on Unfinished Busine8s.
A Committee on Finance and .Accounts.
A Committee on Foreign Correspondence.
A Committee on Dispensations and Charters.
A Committee on Work.
A Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence.
A Committee on Education.
A Committee on By-Laws.
ARTICLE VII.
UIUND OF~'ICERS.

SECTION I. The Grand Master, or, in the event of his absence from the
State, or inability from any cause, the Deputy Grand Master, may, upon

the petition of seven or more Master Masons, properly recommended by the
nearest or most convenient Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons, working
under Charter, grant Dispensations to form new Lodges within the limits of this
State, or in the adjoining Teu!tories, where no Grand Lod~e exists · which Dispensation shall be returnable at the next Annual Commumcation of the Grand
Lodge, when the Grand Lodge may order a perpetual Charter, or continue the
Dispensation until the next Annual Meeting of the Grand Lodge: Provided,
That when application is made for a Dispensation to form a new Lodge in u
town or city, the recommendation of a majority of all the Lodges in such town
or city shall, in every instance, accompany the petition ; and no Dispensation
shall be Issued to the :petitioners, unless their petition be also accompanied by
the certificate of the Worshipful Master of each Lodge recommending it, that
the Worshipful Master named in said petition is fully competent to confer the
three degrees of Masonry.
SEC. 2. On the first day of the Annual Meeting of the Grand Lodge, or as
~oon thereafter as possible, the Grand Master shall lay before the Grand Lodge
a written message, therein detailing un account of his official acts during the
recese, and the state and condition of Masonry in his jurisdiction ; and shall
recommend to the Grand Lodge such measures as he may deem expedient and
necessary.
SEC. 3. The Deputy Grand Master shall also report, In writing, at every Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, all his acts und doings, relating to
.,,.,
his office during the vacation.
SEC. 4. The Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary and Grand Tyler shall receive
such compensation for their services as the Grand Lodge may, from time to time,
determine.
SEc. 5. It shall be the duty of the Grand Secretary to pay over to the Grand
Treasurer all moneys in his hands belonging to the Grand Lodge, at each .Annual Communication, nnd quarterly during the recess thereof; and render an
account of the same at each Annual Meeting of the Grand Lodge.
SEc. 6. The Grand Treasurer shall receive all moneys from the Grand Secretary, belonring to the Grand Lodge, keep a correct record thereof, and at each
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, shall render. an account of all his
receipts and disbursements; but no disbursement shall be made by him without
an order from the Gr·and Lodge, signed by the presiding officer and the Grand
Secretary, except as hereinafter provided.
SEO. 7. The Grand Secretary and Grl\nd Treasurer, prior to their installation,
shall execute, respectively, to the Grand Master, or, in his absence, to the Deputy
Grand Master, for the time being, to the use of the Grand Lodge, a bond, with
such security a,nd for such sum as the Grand Master, or, in his absence, the
Deputy Grand Master, may approve, conditioned for the faithftd discharge or
their respective duties.
Szo. 8. All other Grand Officers receiving funds belonging to the Grand
Lodge, 11hall immediately transmit the same to the Grand Secretary.
ARTICLE VIII.
row1m..~ Oh' ·rHE <HtAND r,oum;.

811:<,"i'ION I. The Grand Lodge has original and exclusive jurisdiction over all
subject. of Masonic legislation, and appellate jurisdiction only from the decisions of the subordinate Lodges; and its .inactments and decisions upon all
questions shall be the supreme Masonic law of the State. It shall also prescribe
such rules and regulations for· the government of the subordinate Lodges, a11
will, in its judgment, conduce to the welfare, prosperity and happiness of the
Craft ; and may grant Dispensations and Charters for the establishment of new
Lodges, and may revoke and annul the same, for such causes us it may deem
sufficient. It shall prescribe the manner, and shall require a uniform mode of
working; and may require from.the subordinate LodgeS:snch reasonable dues and
fees, as will at all times discharge the engagements of the Grand Lodge. •

ARTICLE IX.
REVENUE.
SECTION 1. The fee for instituting a subordinate Lodge, shall be one hundred
and twenty-five dollars; seventy-five dollars of which shall be paid on the issuing of the Dispensation, and fifteen dollars to the Grand Secretary; and fifty
dollars when the Charter is granted, and ten dollarR to the Grand Secretary for
engrossing the same, and affixing thereunto the seal of the Grand Lodge.
SEC. 2. Each Lodge shall pay into the treasury ot' the Grand Lodge the sum
of one dollar for each degree conferred on candidates, the sum of one dollar for
each adjoining member, and one dollar annually for each contributing member.
· SEC. 3. There shall be paid into the hands of the Grand Secretary five dollars
by the applicant, for every diploma granted to 11 member of a Subordinate
Lodge, (four dollars for the Grand Secretary ;) but no diploma shall issue
except upon the presentation of' a oertificate from the Secretary of the Lodge,
of which the applicant is a member, of his good and regular standing therein.

Grand Master, and countersigned by the Grand Secretary, who shall affix thereto
the seal of the Grand Lodge.

SECTION I.
Whenever a member of a Lodge, or any Mason under this jurisdiction, shall
be accused of an offence which, if proved, would subject him to suspension or
expulsion, the proceeding in the premises shall be conducted agreeably to the
following rules : Ruu: 1. The accusation ahall be made in wrlting, over the signature of a
Master Mason, and given In charge of the Secretary of the Lodge, who, under
the direction of the Master, shall serve, or cause the accused to be served, with
an attested copy of the charges, at least ten days previous to the time appolnte<l
for the examination : Provided, That the residence of the accused shall be known ,
and shall be within the distance of fifty miles of the place where the Lodge,
having the matter in hand, Is locate«. If the residence of the accused be at a
greater distance than fifty mile~. but within the State, then, and In that ca11e, l\
summons to appear and show cause, forwarded to him by mail, or ·other conveyance, at least twenty days before the time of trial, shall be considered sufficient
service. If his residence be out of the State, or unknown, the Lodge may proceed to examine the charges, ex parte; but if known, and out of the State, a
Rummons shall be sent him by mail, or otherwise, at least four months before
the time appomted for the examination.
Rur.E "l. The examination of the charges shall be had in a· Lodge ·specially
notified and convened for the purpose, at which no visitors shall be admitted,
except as counsel or witnesses.
· RCLl!l 3. The accused .may select any brother for his counsel, and the witnesses shall testify, if Masons, on their honor as such. Hearsay evidence shall
be excluded. ·
RuLE 4. The question, " Is the accused guilty or not guilty?" shall be distinctly put to each member of the Lodge, and the vote thereon shall be by ballot.
Rur.E 5. If the verdict be eu~penslon or expulsion,,the name of the person so
Ruspeuded or expelled shall be sent np at the ensuing meeting of the Grand
Lodge for exammation ; 1rnd if no appeal be taken, the action shall be final.
RuLE 6. A sentence of expulsion shall not take effect until confirmed by this
Grand Lodge, but eball operate as a suspension of the delinquent, in the meantime. In all cases, 11 vote of two-thirds shall be necesaary to find a verdict of
guilty, and and a like vote shall be required to suspend or expel ; buta majority
!!hall be sufficient to reprimand or censure. When the sentence is expulsion, even
if no appeal be taken, a complete transcript of the proceedings and evidence
shall be sent up to the Grand Lodge.
RULE 7. When 11 sentence of expulsion or suspension shall be pronounced by
any Lodge, the Secretary of such Lodge, under its seal, shall immediately notify
the Grand Secretary of such event.
SECTION II.
Ui;r,E 1. A suspension or expulsion of a Mason from a Royal Arch Chapter,
or a Commandery of Knights Templal', shall not operate as an expulsion from
the Lodge of which he iR a member.
